textes.Chak s'entraîne au jeu de balle même la: Chak practises the ball game even at night. He broke two of Ix Chab's pots. She chased him all the way to the Cenote.
Chak calls himself the best player on the island. He also says I became an astronomer because of a ball to the head. It's not true. I was already an astronomer. The ball just confirmed the stars.
textes.Chak se vante de pouvoir battre les Seig: Chak boasts that he could beat the Lords of Xibalba. You don't joke about the Lords of Death. He plays well, I admit. He talks badly, I observe.
textes.Chak, c'est le meilleur joueur de balle: Chak is the best ball player in Yaxché! And on the whole island! Well, in Yaxché. He gave me his first ball. When I grow up, I'll be like him. But better. I don't tell him that, though.
textes.Chak, le joueur de balle, dit qu'il pour: Chak the ball player says he could beat the Lords of Xibalba. Chak says a lot of things. He took a ball to the head as a kid.
Chak. Your ball stays away from my pots.
textes.Chak. Toujours prêt à défier Xibalba ?: Chak. Still ready to challenge Xibalba?
textes.Chambre sept… non, elle est prise. Chamb: Room seven… no, it's taken. Room nine, sea view. Good night.
textes.Champion à seize ans : une coupe en bois: Champion at sixteen: a cup carved from mother-oak wood, my first. Then a second, then a third. Two years ago, Éclair was leading up to the root bend. She slipped on a wet root. I jumped right over her without stopping, and I won. That's racing. Hop hop. That's racing.
textes.Champs de Blé Dur\nIci pousse le blé des:
Durum Wheat Fields
This is where pasta wheat grows.
No pasta without wheat, no wheat without sun.
textes.Chante-le pendant que je pétris, ça lui: Sing it while I knead; it'll do it good.
textes.Chante-moi la basse, Nausicaa. Celle de: Sing me the low tide, Nausicaa. My mother's.
textes.Chanter faux, j'espère ? C'est mieux, fa: Off-key, I hope? It's better off-key.
textes.Chanter ma chanson à moi, à la prochaine: To sing my own song at the next Dawn festival, from the first word to the last. And to have Caelan accompany me without running off. Or let him run off, why not. This time, I'll know what to do.
textes.Chanter un jour à la surface, au soleil,: To sing one day at the surface, in the sun, and hear the whale answer from close by. And for Triton to be there. Not on watch. Just there.
textes.Chanter, une seule fois, un grand air d': To sing, just once, a great opera aria in the square. Django on guitar, all of Port-Azur on the café terraces, and nobody laughing. Nobody! Not even Colette.
textes.Chapitre trois, Mademoiselle. C'est très: Chapter three, Miss. It's very dense.
textes.Chaque année, Aristide m'invite à la tri: Every year, Aristide invites me onto the platform at the harbour festival. I bring my tape measure. During his speech, I unroll it, slowly, to measure. At the end, I whisper to him: “Two minutes too long.” This year he cut it down. I measured anyway. A minute and a half too long. He's improving.
textes.Chaque année, Grimli et Borin viennent m: Every year, Grimli and Borin come and ask me to judge their beards. I make them wait side by side, in the full wind, for as long as it takes to milk three goats. Then I walk around them, tug a hair here, a hair there, and say: “I win.” Croâ applauds. They leave together, furious.
textes.Chaque année, Orsik m'apporte la facture: Every year, Orsik brings me the bill for the crown. I read it, fold it in four and tuck it into my beard. I have ninety. Ulfa says my beard crackles when I walk. That's the sound of debt. A king never forgets. He files.
textes.Chaque année, au Diable Repu, nous faiso: Every year, at the Diable Repu, we have an arm-wrestling match. One year, she won. Everyone shouted, and I cried. Not because I'd lost: because she was so happy. I told her I'd let her win. That's not quite true. It's not quite false either.
textes.Chaque année, au Diable Repu, on fait un: Every year, at the Diable Repu, Gorgoth and I have an arm-wrestling match. The whole tavern places bets. Once, I won. Gorgoth said he'd let me win. Then he cried. I still don't know if it was from losing or from being happy for me. With him, both are possible.
textes.Chaque année, au Grand Troc, quand la ch: Every year, at the Great Swap, when the chain reaches me, I hold out coins. Two lovely coins. And every year, my uncle pretends to faint, a paw on his forehead. The whole Circle applauds. Then he gets up, gives me back my coins and hands me a pebble. The chain goes on. It's never broken because of me.
textes.Chaque année, au printemps, Colette s'as: Every year, in spring, Colette sits at my table, puts down her coins without counting them and says: “Well?” I predict a great love for her. She shrugs and leaves. Fifteen years running. It's the only price she's never argued over. A grocer who doesn't haggle, traveller: now that's a sign.
textes.Chaque année, j'invite Cendrin à parler: Every year, I invite Cendrin to talk to the new pupils about the patience of fire. He talks for ten minutes, very slowly. Then I spend an hour explaining what he meant. The pupils think he talks too little, and I far too much. I believe they're right on both counts.
textes.Chaque année, je l'invite à la tribune d: Every year, I invite him onto the platform at the harbour festival. He comes with his tape measure. During my speech, I see him unrolling the tape, discreetly, in time with my sentences. At the end, he whispers: “Two minutes too long, Mr Mayor.” Last year, a minute and a half. I'm improving.
textes.Chaque année, je lui demande de m'accomp: Every year, I ask him to accompany me for one song, just one, at the harbour festival. Every year, he refuses. And every year, when it's time to cut the ribbon, I shout: “Django, music!” And he plays. He's never missed once. That, you see, is friendship. He'll never admit it.
textes.Chaque année, je présente au roi la fact: Every year, I present the king with the bill for the crown. Every year, he reads it, folds it in four, says “A king never forgets”, and tucks it into his beard. There are ninety of them in that beard. One day, I'll cut it off while he sleeps. To get my bills back.
textes.Chaque année, l'air de rien, je demande: Every year, casual as you like, I ask Dagna if Sigrun's eating properly up there. She says yes. I say: “Sigrun? Never heard of her.” And I scuttle off to the cellar before she sees my face. Dagna usually sees everything. But this time, she says nothing. That's why I love her.
textes.Chaque année, la première sardine de la: Every year, Driss brings me the first sardine of the season at the end of the jetty. He lays it on the stone, next to my line. He says nothing. I say nothing. He leaves. Fatima grills it that same evening. It's the only sardine I bring home without going by Zohra's.
textes.Chaque année, le jour anniversaire de mo: Every year, on the anniversary of the day I arrived, I bring Léon a punch aboard the Swallow. We drink it on deck, without talking, looking at the village across the water. He shows me my return ticket, still tucked inside his compass. I tell him: “Keep it a little longer.” That's five punches now.
textes.Chaque année, le jour de mon anniversair: Every year, on my birthday, it snows. Only over my house. A little grey cloud, right over my roof, all day long. I know it's him. He says it's the weather. The weather doesn't know my birthday, Borée!
textes.Chaque année, le lendemain de la fête du: Every year, the day after the harbour festival, I offer him a rematch, in front of witnesses. I play badly on purpose: I roll into the gutter, I shoot into the plane trees. He wins. He shouts: “See! I was the best!” And off he goes, happy. It's the best politics I know.
textes.Chaque année, le soir où Gaspard n'est p: Every year, on the evening Gaspard didn't come home, I play his favourite song, an old whaler's lament. Very slowly. The first year, I played it without knowing. Mama put down her tea towel, listened to the end, then brought me a soup without a word. I understood. I play it every year. She's never asked me to.
textes.Chaque année, nous faisons un concours d: Every year, we hold a shouting contest at the port. Usually, Hurla wins. Last year, I shouted “MACKEREL!” so loud that a ship out at sea thought it was being called and turned back. I won. Hurla didn't say a word all day. It was the quietest day in the history of Pandémonia.
textes.Chaque année, on fait la Course de la Ba: Every year, we hold the Balafre Race: round the island, quay to quay. Last year, his bowsprit got caught in my shrouds on the last turn. We came in stuck together like two crabs. Each of us says he won. Mama Grog settled it: both captains buy the round. We're still paying.
textes.Chaque année, on fait un concours de cri: Every year, Moloka and I hold a shouting contest at the port. Usually, I win. Last year, she shouted “MACKEREL!” so loud that a ship out at sea thought it was being called and turned back. She won. I didn't say a word for a whole day. Everyone thought I was ill.
textes.Chaque année, pour l'anniversaire de Neb: Every year, for Nebet's birthday, Mérit makes a honey cake shaped like Miou, with the crooked ear. She spends the whole morning on it. She says it's for Nebet. But I've seen her set aside the best ear. For herself. Mérit has always loved ears.

Every year, for Nebet's birthday, I make a honey cake shaped like Miou, crooked ear and all. The first year, Nebet refused to eat it: “You don't eat Miou!” Now she starts with the tail, so Miou won't feel anything. Tiyi cries with laughter every time.
textes.Chaque année, pour l'anniversaire de not: Every year, on the anniversary of the day we met, Tic makes me a new backwards watch. And every year, I put it in the Bazaar's window, for thirty coins. He walks past, puts his hand on his heart and cries scandal. Then he comes back in the evening to help me wind it. They all sell. Except the first one: I wear it.
textes.Chaque année, pour mon anniversaire, Sér: Every year, for my birthday, Séraphine leaves a ladder in front of the library, with a ribbon. Forty ladders in forty years. I give them all to Mathurin, who turns them into planks for the jetty. She says she walks all over my birthdays. I say it's the most useful of her presents.
textes.Chaque année, pour son anniversaire, il: Every year, on her birthday, it snows over her house. Only her house. A little cloud, all day long. She thinks it's me. I have nothing to say about that. The weather is a fickle thing. Hm.
textes.Chaque année, à l'anniversaire de notre: Every year, on the anniversary of the day we met, I make her a new backwards watch. And every year, she puts it in the Bazaar's window. I protest, for form's sake: “My love watch, in a shop window!” She says love is for sharing. The first one, she never sold. She wears it on her wrist.
textes.Chaque année, à la fin de la saison, Hec: Every year, at the end of the season, Hector and I redo the sums for the sign on a corner of the counter: how many fizzes, how many evenings, how many mugs. It's been paid off for twelve years. Every year, we look at the result, we look at each other, and we keep quiet. I pour him a fizz. “On the sign.”
textes.Chaque année, à la fête de la Forge, il: Every year, at the Forge Festival, he raises his mug to me and shouts: “No hard feelings, Bramm!” Every year, I don't raise mine. That's a hundred and twenty festivals. He never tires of it. Neither do I.
textes.Chaque année, à la même date, j'envoie a: Every year, on the same date, I send the Professor a little card: “The book awaits you. No hurry.” I change one word each time, to see if he reads them. Last year, I wrote: “The book awaits you. It's getting wrinkles.” He answered with four pages on the wrinkles of books. I filed them.
textes.Chaque année, à la rentrée, Malachar m'i: Every year, at the start of term, Malachar invites me to talk to the new students about “the patience of fire”. I talk for ten minutes. He talks for an hour, to explain what I meant. The students fall asleep. So do I, a little. It's a fine tradition.
textes.Chaque après-midi, je lui apporte son th: Every afternoon I bring him his tea and we play draughts on an old carved board. He keeps a piece up his sleeve. I've seen it for twenty years: when he's losing, he scratches his wrist, and an extra piece appears on the board. I say nothing. Once, I counted: he had fourteen pieces. We each have twelve.
textes.Chaque arbre-maison a un nom. Celui d'Il: Every tree-house has a name. Ilyria's is called “Dawn-Thread”. Mine is called “Still-Standing”. It's an old elvish word.
textes.Chaque automne, Tobias monte sur mon toi: Every autumn, Tobias climbs up on my roof, well, on my boat's keel, and plugs the cracks with hot tar. The whole beach smells of tar. I hand him a mackerel, he says “no need”, he takes it anyway. Thirty years now. Thirty mackerel. I owe him nothing, he owes me nothing. It's perfect.
textes.Chaque automne, je recalfate le toit de: Every autumn, I recaulk Fañch's roof, well, the keel of his boat. He hands me a mackerel, I say “no need”, I take it. One autumn, he handed me a lobster. I got scared: I thought he was ill. He'd just caught too many lobsters. I ate it anyway, warily.
textes.Chaque dimanche, je lui porte des biscui: Every Sunday, I take him gear cookies. I look at his roof, I count his eyebrows, and I ask him how “the Big One” is coming along. He answers “soon!” with shining eyes. I always leave a little worried. And a little proud to have been his pupil. Mostly proud.
textes.Chaque fin d'année, je laisse une boutei: At the end of every year, I leave a bottle of lamp oil at the foot of the lighthouse door. No note, no ribbon. The next morning, the bottle's gone, and that evening Anselme gives me three flashes instead of two. Once a year. It's his way of saying thank you. Or good health. Or both.
textes.Chaque fin d'été, au Cercle, je mène le: Every end of summer, at the Circle, I lead the Great Swap: the whole village swaps in a ring, and the chain mustn't break. Twenty years it held! Last year, it broke between Caramel and Trèfle: the sardine for the carrot bread. Heh heh… I laughed. I didn't sleep. And then my niece Grelot sells for coins, and that fox Roux taunts me. A hard life, my friend.
textes.Chaque fois qu'il parle de la porte, je: Every time he talks about the gate, I set my compass on his map, on Stoneheart. He draws around it. The other evening, I looked more closely: around my compass, he'd written, very small: “Here, the Admiral keeps watch.” I haven't moved the compass since.
textes.Chaque fois qu'il raconte le pirate et l: Every time he tells the tale of the pirate and the treasure in the caves, he says the pirate had a black beard. So I say: “Red.” The whole halqa turns towards me. I say nothing more. He carries on, and he never corrects it. I think he gets it wrong on purpose. I pretend not to believe it. We've been playing that game for sixty years.
textes.Chaque fois qu'un caravanier poli loge c: Every time a polite caravan trader stays with me, I send him to buy a dish from Halima: “Go and see my niece, she has lovely pottery.” She spots them straight away, by their son-in-law look. She sells them the heaviest dish on the stall and sends them back. Twenty-three caravan traders, twenty-three dishes sold, not one wedding. At least she's doing business.
textes.Chaque fois qu'un caravanier un peu poli: Every time a caravan driver with half-decent manners stays at the Fondouk, my aunt has me come over “to deliver a dish”. Once it was a salt merchant, very pushy, who wanted to marry me that very evening. I took the dish I was delivering and dropped it. On purpose. He ran away. My aunt made me pay for the dish. It was worth the price.
textes.Chaque fois qu'un voyageur part vers Ram: Every time a traveller sets off for Ramure, with Mbarek's camels or by Zéphyr, I give him a story for Tilleul. They tell me he tells our night differently: that he's the one who walked three days to my square. Maybe he's right. A story can happen twice. He's the one who taught me that.
textes.Chaque fois que Kevin repêche quelqu'un,: Every time Kevin fishes someone out, I tell all my customers. “You know who saved the gentleman in the hat? My son!” In the time it takes to weigh a sardine, I've already told three rescues. Kevin says I exaggerate. I don't exaggerate. I round up. It's not the same.
textes.Chaque fois que Nimiel tombe, Miriel arr: Every time Nimiel falls, Miriel gets to the shop before her, running. She knows the way to my stool by heart. I give her a cup of tea too: the mother often needs more looking after than the little one.
textes.Chaque fois que Théo passe devant ma bou: Every time Théo walks past my shop, I give him a painted shell. Free! Me! He's counted them: eleven. He lines them up in front of his sandcastles like soldiers. The other day he asked me: “When I've got a hundred, will you give me a kite?” That kid has a head for business. I'll hire him in ten years.
textes.Chaque fois que j'apprends un nouveau mo: Every time I teach the piano a new piece, Philibert is the first to hear it. In the evening, on the promenade, I play him the cylinder in my little test box. He closes his eyes, listens to the very end, and always says: “I hadn't thought of that.” Coming from him, that's the finest compliment there is.
textes.Chaque fois que je cherche mes lunettes,: Every time I'm looking for my glasses, Petit-Pierre comes running and hands them to me. He never says where he found them. One day, I asked him. He said: “On your head.” I didn't believe him. He added: “You never look on your head.” It's true. He's very clever, that boy.
textes.Chaque fois que je parle d'ouvrir la Por: Every time I talk about opening the Gate of the Four Seals, the Admiral sets her compass down on my map, right on Stoneheart, and says: “Closed gates are often closed for a reason, Le Goff.” Then she leaves. I draw around the compass. She leaves it there for a very long time.
textes.Chaque fois que je parle du fantôme du q: Every time I mention the ghost on the fourth floor, Monsieur Edmond goes white and says “Nonsense, mademoiselle, back to work.” Very fast. Too fast. I think he's scared of ghosts. A man his age! I offered him a night light. He dropped his register.
textes.Chaque fois que je passe devant la bouti: Every time I go past the shop, Victor gives me a painted shell. A blue one, a red one, one with a star. I've got eleven! I counted them all by myself, without saying twenty-thousand. I line them up in front of my castle, like soldiers. The blue one's the boss.
textes.Chaque fois que je raconte le pirate et: Every time I tell the tale of the pirate and the treasure in the caves, I say the pirate had a black beard. And every time, from the front row, Fatima says: “Red.” The whole halqa turns towards her. She adds nothing. I could say red. I don't say red. If I said red, she'd never say anything again.
textes.Chaque fois que je rate un sort devant e: Every time I mess up a spell in front of her, the archmage pulls a little notebook out of her sleeve and writes in it. I think it's the list of everything I've broken. It must be three hundred pages by now. One day, she'll hand me the bill. I hope she lets me pay in instalments.
textes.Chaque fois que je vais au quai, Léon me: Every time I go to the quay, Léon lets me ring the Swallow's bell for departure. Once I rang it too early, and the boat left without three gentlemen. They were running with their suitcases! Léon said “The captain decides.” But he went back for them anyway.
Every time, I say: “I leave tomorrow.” She answers: “Good.” The next day, I don't leave. She doesn't ask anything. In the evening she brings my tea up at midnight, as if nothing had happened. Fifteen years now. At the oasis, the camels must think I'm dead. Or married.
textes.Chaque histoire, je la paie une noisette: I pay one hazelnut for each story. That's the price! I put it on his knee at the start. And at the end I take it back as I leave, because there's never an end, so the story isn't finished, so it isn't paid for. Grandpa says I'd make a very good tanuki.
textes.Chaque hiver, Borée vient me remercier p: Every winter, Borée comes to thank me for the bundle of twisted wood he finds at his door. I've never brought him any wood! The first time, I said “don't mention it”, out of politeness. Now it's too late to tell the truth. I really wonder who it is. Someone who gets up early. And has warm hands.
textes.Chaque hiver, quelqu'un dépose un fagot: Every winter, someone leaves a bundle of twisted wood at my door, before dawn. It can only be Mathurin: he's the only one who gets up before me. I thanked him. He looked surprised, said “don't mention it”, then left very quickly. He's modest. That's a virtue.
textes.Chaque inventeur de Cliquetis rate une i: Every inventor in Cliquetis botches one invention out of two. I buy up the failures. They're the most beautiful: they tried.
textes.Chaque jeudi après-midi, Pauline s'assoi: Every Thursday afternoon, Pauline sits at my table with two orange-blossom cakes, one for her, one for me. I read her cards, for free. She tells me about her week at the hotel, for free too. Nobody pays, and everybody wins. It's the most honest business on the promenade.
textes.Chaque jeudi, Madame Rita me tire les ca: Every Thursday, Madame Rita reads my cards, and every Thursday I draw the journey card. Always the same one! She says it's fate. I think the card's got a dog-ear. But it makes me happy anyway: one day, I'll leave. Maybe as far as the end of the street. To open my guesthouse.
textes.Chaque jeudi, Tiburce s'assoit dans la s: Every Thursday, Tiburce sits in the steam room, eyes closed, and says his horns are breathing. One day, I explained that horns don't breathe. He opened one eye and replied: “Yours, perhaps not.” Since then, I keep a separate scented towel for him. He says his horns prefer it.
textes.Chaque jeudi, je vais faire respirer mes: Every Thursday, I go and let my horns breathe in the steam of the Baths. One day, Bulle told me horns didn't breathe. I replied: “Yours, perhaps not.” He laughed for ten minutes. Since then, he keeps a scented towel aside for me. He says my horns prefer it. They do prefer it.
textes.Chaque jour à midi, Asmodin aligne mes b: Every day at noon, Asmodin lines up my brioches on the counter and measures them one by one with his silver ruler. There's always a crooked one. He frowns. I look innocent. One day, he pretended not to see it. So the next day, I made two crooked ones. He sighed very loudly. It was almost a laugh.
textes.Chaque jour à midi, je viens chercher le: Every day at noon, I come to fetch the palace brioches. I measure them with my silver ruler: they must all be the same height. There is always one, just one, that leans. Monsieur Bobor puts on an innocent air. One day, I pretended not to see it. The next day, there were two.
textes.Chaque jour, il vient voir son tapis. Il: Every day, he comes to see his carpet. He corrects a cliff with the tip of his sabre, he grumbles, he pays, he leaves. One day, a customer asked him what it was. The captain said: “A pirate's prayer rug.” The customer asked what pirates pray for. The captain answered: “That nobody asks them questions.”
textes.Chaque jour, je passe voir mon tapis. Il: Every day, I drop by to see my rug. It's never right. That cliff is too round, that rock too far left. I correct it with the tip of my sabre, thread by thread. Samira watches me, arms crossed. Yesterday she said: “You know this coast very well, for a rug.” I told her to weave.
textes.Chaque lundi, je glisse un mot sous la p: Every Monday, I slip a note under the harbour office door: “Lemonade tonight? Fernand.” She puts it away in a drawer, without answering. Apparently she's kept them all. Hundreds of little notes. Every week I invite her, every week she says no. And on Sunday, she comes.
textes.Chaque matin, Brume me rapporte ce qu'el: Every morning Brume tells me what she's read: round footprints at the edge of the big pond, going into the water and never coming out. I listen, I nod, I say nothing. She can tell I know something. She's right. But it's not for me to tell her.
textes.Chaque matin, Céleste m'apporte la météo: Every morning, Céleste brings me the star forecast, handwritten: “Clear sky, rising moon, a shooting star around three.” I pin it up next to the counter. Customers read it with their coffee; some come specially. I don't understand all of it. But I like knowing it'll be fine up there.
textes.Chaque matin, Dwalin descend le chaudron: Every morning, Dwalin carries Dagna's cauldron down to the Mug, and I resell her stew at twice what she charges. At the Forge Festival, I give her the difference in a little embroidered purse, with a note: “For the salt.” She laughs about it for a week. Borin doesn't find it funny.
textes.Chaque matin, Gorgoth garde les chiots p: Every morning, Gorgoth minds the puppies while I fetch the fish scraps from Moloka's. They climb on him like a mountain. He doesn't move a whisker, so they don't fall off. The greatest champion on the island. The gentlest of mountains.
textes.Chaque matin, Lumi me prête dix lucioles: Every morning, Lumi lends me ten fireflies, and I do my rounds. I give the first drop to the queen's flower. I water Noisette's pots, and her cactus, one drop a month. Then Zéphyr flies three times around the Tree, my drops fall, and I start again. Gently. You must always start again gently.
textes.Chaque matin, Moulay Brahim me donne le: Every morning, Moulay Brahim gives me the price, and I round it up a little, for the music. Zohra, under my platform, refuses my sea bream. The pirates' cook buys up everything that's left. Afterwards, twelve sardines at Mustapha's, for the voice. And in the evening, I sing on the square. When Hamid's there, we sing louder than necessary. The lanterns shake. They're used to it.
textes.Chaque matin, Plumette passe par le marc: Every morning Plumette flies over the market, even though it's not on her way at all. She hovers a second over my stall and calls out: “Nothing for you today!” Then off she goes. I asked her why the detour. She said: “So you don't wait for nothing.” She's kind, for an owl.
textes.Chaque matin, Tobias passe devant la tav: Every morning, Tobias walks past the tavern at seven, and every morning I slip a rolled-up crêpe into his apron pocket. He pretends not to notice. In the evening, he brings me back the paper, folded in four, nice and clean. Thirty years of folded papers. I keep them in a box. I don't know why.
textes.Chaque matin, elle pose une fleur sur mo: Every morning, she puts a flower on my desk at the calmecac. Never the same one. One day, I wanted to paint them all in a codex. I'd need a hundred pages. She said: “Then paint fast, I've still got seeds.” I'm on the eightieth flower. She's already planted the next hundred.
textes.Chaque matin, elle vient avec sa pelle c: Every morning, she comes with her shovel to fetch embers for the Great Forge. I grumble: “The sacred fire is not a stove!” She replies: “A fire that's good for nothing gets bored!” It's been going on for thirty years. The day she doesn't come, I think I'll be the one who's bored.
textes.Chaque matin, il cherche sa couronne par: Every morning, he looks everywhere for his crown: under the throne, behind the banners. I step up and say, very quietly: “Majesty… your head.” He raises his hand. There it is. Once, he looked for it twice in a row, on purpose, I think. I said “your head” twice. He looked very pleased.
textes.Chaque matin, il s'installe sur le banc: Every morning, he settles on the next bench and tunes his guitar. And I tap the beat with the tip of my foot, without thinking. One day he stopped dead and said: “Don't move, you're my metronome.” Since then, he looks at my foot before he starts. That's a great responsibility, at my age.
textes.Chaque matin, il vient compter ses trois: Every morning he comes to count his three carrots in front of my stall. One. Two. Three. Slowly, looking at me, to tease me. One day I put a fourth carrot on the counter, without a word. He stared at it for a whole minute. He didn't take it. But his ears went all hot.
textes.Chaque matin, il y a un billet de Célest: Every morning, there's a note from Céleste under my door. “Calm night, three coughs, heading north-east.” “Two coughs. West wind. He was singing, I think.” I keep them all in a hatbox. It's almost full. I hope he lands before I have to buy a second one.
textes.Chaque matin, je cherche ma couronne. Ch: Every morning, I look for my crown. Every morning, Gunnar steps up, clears his throat and says, very low: “Majesty… your head.” I raise my hand. There it is. Once, I looked for it twice on purpose, just to see. He said “your head” twice, without smiling. The perfect guard.
textes.Chaque matin, je commande six croissants: Every morning, I order six croissants. Madame Margaux picks the goldenest and sets them aside before I even arrive. Once, there was an overbaked one in the bag, by mistake. She ran all the way to the jetty to swap it. The seagulls were waiting. They can't tell the difference, you know. I can.
textes.Chaque matin, je cueille la rosée de lun: Every morning I gather moon dew from the roots and water the village flowers with it. It's a small job, but an important one.
textes.Chaque matin, je cueille la rosée sur le: Every morning I gather the dew from the roots and water the village flowers, one by one. Grommelot pretends not to see me go by. Mélisse takes my moon dew for her tea. And Zéphyr brings me Perlée's letters… always full of advice. I read them twice. The second time, I cry a little.
textes.Chaque matin, je descends au Cénote pour: Every morning, I go down to the Cenote for the offerings. Then I pray at the top of Kukulkan, I watch over the stela with Ah Kin Pech, and in the evening I climb to the Venus platform. Little Kinich follows me with his questions, Chak boasts about taking on Xibalba, and Yum Kab brings me the honey for the balché. The Feathered Serpent has a lot to do. So do I.
textes.Chaque matin, je donne la première brioc: Every morning I give the first brioche to Grandpa Ébène, in exchange for a story. It's been going on for forty years. I've never told him I already knew half his stories. He tells them so well the second time.
textes.Chaque matin, je donne mes restes de poi: Every morning I give my fish scraps to Flammèche for her puppies. One of the puppies stole a whole grouper from me once. He dragged it all the way to the kennel. He was so proud I didn't dare scold him.
textes.Chaque matin, je dépose une goutte sur c: Every morning I place a drop on every flower in the kingdom. There are four thousand three hundred and two. I know them all.
textes.Chaque matin, je fais trois tours de l'A: Every morning, I do three laps of the Tree before breakfast. It's my exercise. And every morning, Perlée looks at me with her calm, calm eyes, in the middle of her drops on the ground. She never shouts. That's worse. Once, I only did two laps. She thanked me. I felt ashamed all day.
textes.Chaque matin, je garde les chiots pendan: Every morning, I mind the pups while Flammèche goes to fetch fish scraps from Moloka's. They climb all over me, roll around in my beard, chew on my horns. I don't move, so as not to make them fall. Once, they all fell asleep on me. I stayed sitting until noon. I missed a fight.
textes.Chaque matin, je lis ses traces d'entraî: Every morning, I read her training tracks from the night. I know where she runs, how many laps, where she slips. I don't tell anyone. But at the root bend, where she fell two years ago, I tracked down the best foothold: a flat stone, hidden under the moss. I showed it to her without a word. She runs on it every night.
textes.Chaque matin, je lui apporte le premier: Every morning I bring her the first fish. Not for the stall: for her. She says “Mrrr, Dad, again?” and takes it anyway. Three years ago, the first morning after Ardoise left, I brought two. She said nothing. She ate both.
textes.Chaque matin, je monte au palais avec un: Every morning I go up to the palace with a warm cracker. The queen eats it with her eyes closed, in silence, down to the last crumb. One morning I asked her what she found in it. She said: “The taste of the first night. The one when your grandmother saved us.” I went back down, and I didn't sell a thing all morning.
textes.Chaque matin, je passe par le marché exp: Every morning, I go through the market on purpose to call out “Nothing for you today!” to Grelot. She throws me an apple. On days when there's a card, I don't say anything, I put it on her stall. Two years ago, I put something else there. She asked me for a promise. I'm keeping it. It weighs more than my satchel.
textes.Chaque matin, je passe à la boulangerie: Every morning, I go by the bakery to count the croissants. For the investigation. And I take one “for inspection”, to check there's nothing abnormal about them. There's nothing abnormal about them. I check anyway. Rigour is an everyday thing.
textes.Chaque matin, je pose une fleur sur son: Every morning, I put a flower on her desk. She says she's going to paint them all. She's up to the eightieth. I told her I'd planted the next hundred. She sighed. I think she's pleased. With Citlali, sighs are often joy.
textes.Chaque matin, je vais chercher les reste: Every morning, I fetch fish scraps from Moloka's, at the port, while Gorgoth minds my pups. He doesn't move a hair when they climb all over him. Then I feed them, brush them, walk them. In the evening, they bark at the street lamps, and Nox says good evening to them. Little Pépin comes to recite their birthdays.
textes.Chaque matin, le Lord entre, soulève son: Every morning, the Lord comes in, lifts his straw hat and says: “Six, my dear.” I pick him the most golden ones. He eats one on my doorstep, eyes closed. The other five he takes to the pier and crumbles for the seagulls. I've never dared ask why. It's prettier not knowing.
textes.Chaque matin, le brigadier passe « vérif: Every morning, the sergeant drops by to “check everything is in order”. He takes a croissant, “for inspection”. He inspects it down to the last crumb. I offered to let him pay for it. He said: “That would be bribery, madam.”
textes.Chaque matin, on fait la course jusqu'à: Every morning, we race to the channel. One day, I was three lengths ahead. Youssef shouted: “WHALE!” I turned round. It was a barrel. He overtook me while I was looking at the barrel. Since then, I don't turn round. Even for a real one, I won't turn round. Too bad for me.
textes.Chaque matin, papa m'apporte le premier: Every morning, Dad brings me the first fish of the day. Not for the stall: for me, like a present. Even a measly little sardine. He puts it on my apron, says “shh”, and off he goes. He's never missed a morning. Except the day of the cold. That day, I brought him a skewer in bed.
textes.Chaque matin, quand j'ai fini de poser m: Every morning, when I've finished setting down my drops, Zéphyr whistles past. Fffwoosh. Hundreds of drops on the ground. I start again, in the same order, gently. One day, I asked him to do his rounds later. He replied: “Later is for snails.”
textes.Chaque matin, quand je passe sous la Ska: Every morning, when I pass under the Skala, I take off my tricorn and bow all the way to the ground: “A very good day to you, caïd!” He grits his teeth. One day, I brought him up a bottle of Mama Lou's rum, “between guardians of the sea”. He emptied it into the sea in front of me. I said: “The fish are going to be in a good mood.” I still greet him. Lower.
textes.Chaque matin, quand je rentre me coucher: Every morning, when I go home to bed, I meet Mother Brasille on her way to the garden. She says “good night”, I say “good morning”, and she slips a sprig of ash mint into my pocket. One day, she was ill and didn't come. I couldn't sleep. I was the one who took her her herbal tea. For once.
textes.Chaque maître enseigne un sort : Aurélie: Each master teaches one spell: Aurélien light, Pyra fire, Borée frost, Zéphyrine levitation, Théophraste telekinesis, Mother Sage healing. Learn all six, and I'll present you with your staff at the Circle.
textes.Chaque midi, Brindille se pose sur le re: Every noon, Brindille lands on my windowsill, demands a Brasier coffee and tells me all the city's news in one minute. I pay her with the coffee; she pays me with the news. In the evening, I tell it to the sailors. Hurla claims she's the one who gives out the news. Me, I serve it with the punch.
textes.Chaque midi, je lève ma tasse au moment: Every noon, I raise my cup at the moment of the whistle. If it's on the dot, Gaston gives it to me free. I haven't paid for my coffee in four years. And in the evening, from my window, I hear the long eleven o'clock whistle. Always on the dot too. A valve doesn't whistle on time by itself. I've never asked anything. Some whistles are nobody's business.
textes.Chaque midi, je raconte à Grumbald toute: Every noon, I tell Grumbald all the city's news, in one minute, between two sips of coffee. In the evening, he tells it to the sailors over grog. One day, I told him a made-up piece of news, just to see. By evening, the whole tavern knew it. The next day, Hurla was shouting it on the square. I've never lied again.
textes.Chaque mois, Lucie me dessine la coque v: Every month, Lucie draws me the hull seen from below, with the spots where the wood is soft. She always adds fish in the corners, I don't know why. I file her drawings in the black book, with the hole numbers. I've never rubbed out the fish. The book is less sad with them.
textes.Chaque mois, je fais le tour de la coque: Every month, I go all round the hull from underneath, and I draw Tobias the spots where the wood is soft. He files the drawings in his black notebook, with the numbers of the holes. He has hundreds. Mine are the only ones with fish in the corners. He's never said anything. He keeps them anyway.
textes.Chaque motif raconte quelque chose : le: Every pattern tells something: the serpent, the maize, the diamond of the world with its four corners. A huipil is a book you wear.
textes.Chaque nuit de traversée, quand L'Hirond: Every crossing night, when the Swallow rounds the point, Léon raises his lantern. Twice. I answer with two beams. It means: I see you, you see me. One night, he did three. I kept watch, worried, until dawn. Odette told me he was celebrating his boat's fortieth birthday. I'd answered him with three beams. Just the once.
textes.Chaque nuit, Rê traverse le monde d'en d: Every night, Ra crosses the underworld in his boat, and Apophis, the serpent of chaos, wants to swallow him. Since the Pyramid of Ra was sealed, Néferet no longer hears Ra singing at dawn.
textes.Chaque nuit, en rentrant de chez Toni, j: Every night, on my way back from Toni's, I play a little song on the ukulele under Rose's window. To say goodnight. For a year, I thought she liked it. Then I noticed that her shutter always closed at midnight on the dot. Just before the first note.
textes.Chaque nuit, en rentrant de ma table, je: Every night, on my way home from my table, I find a bowl of soup under a tea towel on her windowsill. I eat it standing up, in the street, at four in the morning. I leave a coin in the bowl. We've never talked about it. If she stopped, I don't think I'd know how to get home any more.
textes.Chaque nuit, je tiens le petit tambour d: Every night, I play the Circle's little drum. Roux taught me the rhythms of Tazira: boom, boom-boom! I practise behind the bakery, because Bondi, my neighbour, says I keep him awake before races. After every party, I argue about the tempo with Bourru, and Lilas asks me to play softer. I promise. Then the moon rises out of the pond, and boom!
textes.Chaque nuit, quelqu'un emprunte un recue: Every night, someone borrows a book of poems through the window and brings it back before dawn. They sign the register with a single word: “Thank you”. I know it's Nox. I leave the window open, and a candle lit.
textes.Chaque pouvoir lancé rend de l'endurance: Every power you cast gives back stamina; every four powers, half a heart.
textes.Chaque premier lundi du mois, je passe c: On the first Monday of every month, I call on Isaac and buy his entire stock of loaded dice. Twenty-five coins a die. Then I go down to the quay and throw them into the bay, one by one. The bottom of the harbour must be carpeted with them. Isaac says I'm his best customer. I say he's my worst supplier. We're both right.
textes.Chaque printemps, Dwalin me descend un t: Every spring, Dwalin brings me down a barrel with no name, no note, nothing. I tell everyone I don't know where it comes from. I taste it alone, door shut. It's golden, it smells of warm bread from Dagna's oven. It's better than mine. The first one to repeat that gets cut off from the foam for life.
textes.Chaque printemps, Jos et moi, on étale m: Every spring, Jos and I spread my map out at the tavern and prepare the expedition: ropes, lanterns, file, crêpes. We toast to setting off. The next day, I've always got a good reason to put it off: the wind, the rain, a coastline to correct. Jos says nothing. He nods. He's a true friend.
textes.Chaque printemps, Matthias et moi, on pr: Every spring, Matthias and I plan the expedition to Stoneheart. He unrolls his map on a tavern table, I set my file and magnifying glass on it, we raise our mugs. Next day, he's got a headache from all the planning, and I've got iron in the fire. We put it off till the following year. That's nine years now.
textes.Chaque printemps, Pyrus vient négocier l: Every spring, Pyrus comes to haggle over the price of the Guard's swords. “Guard price,” he says. I say: “Kraxx price.” We argue for an hour. I always slip a whetstone into the package, without a word. He thinks it's a sales gift. It's a bit more than that.
textes.Chaque printemps, Sigrun remplit le prem: Every spring, Sigrun fills the first barrel of the year and has it taken down to the Blazing Mug, with no name on it. She thinks nobody knows. Dwalin's the one who carries it. And Dwalin's the one who tells me Ulfa tastes it all alone, door shut, before anyone else.
textes.Chaque printemps, Tobias me remet son ra: Every spring, Tobias hands me his report on the hull: a black notebook, hundreds of hole numbers, and on the last page, always the same word: “Will hold.” One spring, he forgot the word. I spent the night rereading the notebook. The next day, he came back to write it, apologising. He'd simply forgotten.
textes.Chaque printemps, j'inspecte sa chaudièr: Every spring I inspect his copper boiler. Last year, while I was checking the valve, he blew a bubble round my monocle. A small, round, perfect bubble. I kept it for four seconds without blinking. Then I said: “Regulation.” He laughed for the rest of the inspection. The report is very favourable.
textes.Chaque printemps, je lui demande s'il es: Every spring, I ask him if he's ready to forgive Pyra. Every spring, he looks at the lake and answers: “It hasn't finished thinking about it.” Twelve springs. One day, I asked him if the lake was a fast thinker. He looked at me as if I were a first-year apprentice.
textes.Chaque printemps, je m'assieds à sa tabl: Every spring, I sit down at her table. She turns over three cards, she sighs, she says: “A great love, Colette.” I pay. Without haggling. It's the only price in the archipelago I don't argue about. Gisèle says it's my only vice. She forgets the novels.
textes.Chaque printemps, je négocie le prix des: Every spring, I negotiate the price of the Guard's swords. I say “Guard price”. He says “Kraxx price”. We argue for an hour, we come to an agreement, and when I get home I find he's slipped a whetstone into the package. It's his way of saying he likes me. He'll never say it any other way.
textes.Chaque printemps, je pose un bouquet sur: Every spring I leave a bouquet on Aëlwen's counter, tied with gold thread. I never sign it. One morning she'd left a cup of herbal tea beside it, with a note: “For the wind.” I drank it on the spot. The wind enjoyed it very much.
textes.Chaque printemps, je repeins moi-même le: Every spring, I repaint Fernand's mooring number on the quay myself. Number seven. The salt eats it away every winter. He's never asked me why I do it, and I've never told him. That's where Marius moored the boat, every evening.
textes.Chaque printemps, les navets de Père Gau: Every spring, Père Gaubert's turnips wake up and run off across the Southern Fields. With his bad knees, he can't catch a single one any more. He'd like five golden turnips, caught during a Great Turnip Alert.
textes.Chaque printemps, {surnom}, je remplis l: Every spring, {surnom}, I fill the first barrel of the year and send it down to the Blazing Mug, with no name on it. I don't know if Ulfa drinks it or tips it down the gutter. She tells everyone she doesn't know me. I keep doing it anyway. She's the one who taught me everything.
textes.Chaque retour, je trouve un coquillage d: Every time I come back, I find a shell in the net. The prettiest one. I put it on her chair. Without a word. Thirty years. She keeps them in a big jar, by the window. One day, a shell fell. I picked it up. Put it back on top. She saw me. We said nothing. It was good.
textes.Chaque samedi, je pose un régime devant: Every Saturday, I leave a bunch outside Barnabé's hut. Gaston counts it out loud: “One! Two! Three! Shipwreck!” He can only count to three; after that, he says “Shipwreck”. Barnabé says “Gaston, write that down!” and Gaston eats a banana. Rent paid.
textes.Chaque semaine, Bastien me monte son pan: Every week, Bastien brings his basket of fish up to me. We argue over the price of every sardine. He says “Peuchère”, I say “Cash”, and we always end up at last week's price. That's our way of saying hello.
textes.Chaque semaine, Fernand m'invite à l'ani: Every week, Fernand invites me for a glass of his famous lemonade, and every week I refuse. On Sundays, I come. He takes out two glasses and the bottle he hides in a lobster pot. We don't talk much. One Sunday, he made me laugh. He was so surprised he knocked the bottle over.
textes.Chaque semaine, Nadine me tend une envel: Every week, Nadine hands me an envelope, smiling. Too much. A big smile, with all her teeth. As if she knew something I don't. Or that I do. I take the envelope, I say thanks, I go home. She's still smiling behind me. I can feel it on my back.
textes.Chaque semaine, Youssef vient au chantie: Every week, Youssef comes to the yard, sits on a trestle and empties his purse in front of me. He counts. Out loud. “One, two, three…” I pretend not to listen. One week, he had three coins and a sardine. He wanted the sardine to count. I said no. He insisted. It counts as one nail. No more.
textes.Chaque semaine, dans la boîte jaune, je: Every week, in the yellow postbox, I find an envelope addressed “To L., the tall one on the quay”. No name, no street. The tall one on the quay! There's only one in Port-Azur. I slip it into Lucas's letterbox, High Street, whistling, as if nothing were going on. I'm a postwoman, not a gossip. Well, not about that.
textes.Chaque semaine, il m'apporte une « améli: Every week, he brings me an “improvement” in a little pot. Cinnamon and herring. Ship's biscuit. Double salt. I always taste it, to be polite. I shut my eyes very tight and say “unforgettable”. It's true: I can't forget it. Some nights, I still think about it.
textes.Chaque semaine, je demande à Tchoum le p: Every week, I ask Tchoum the name of the twenty-fourth speaker. He says “Later”. I'll tell you a secret, {surnom}: I couldn't care less about speakers. It's to hear him talk. He has a lovely voice, Tchoum, when he lets it out. Two words a week. That's my treasure. Whatever you do, don't tell him.
textes.Chaque semaine, je demande à Zéphyr de q: Every week, I ask Zéphyr which island my hazelnut came from. He thinks, he scratches his head, and he says: “An island with trees.” THEY ALL HAVE TREES! Once, he said: “An island with trees and wind.” I thought we were getting somewhere. Nope.
textes.Chaque semaine, je lui apporte ma plus b: Every week, I bring her my finest perch. For Nebet, who's growing: she needs fish. Once, a lotus flower fell into the basket. All by itself, I don't know how. Tiyi looked at it, then put it in a bowl of water without a word. The lotus lasted a week. I came by to see it every day. The lotus.
textes.Chaque semaine, je lui apporte une « amé: Every week, I bring her an “improvement” to taste, in a little pot. Cinnamon and herring tagine. Ship's biscuit tagine. Double-salt tagine. She always tastes it, out of politeness, and screws her eyes shut very tight. She says it's “unforgettable”. It's the nicest word anyone's ever said to me.
textes.Chaque semaine, je lui échange une lampe: Every week I trade her a mother-of-pearl lamp for a bag of crackers. I eat the crackers, she resells the lamps, supposedly. Ondine, who counts everything, told me there are thirty-seven at her place. Lit. I said nothing. I made the next one a little prettier.
textes.Chaque semaine, je monte mon panier de p: Every week I carry my basket of fish up to Octave's cheese shop. We haggle over the price of every sardine. I say “Well I never”, he says “Cash”, and we always end up at last week's price. Once, I offered a lower price, just to see. He refused. He said it was fishy.
textes.Chaque semaine, je passe chez sa mère, a: Every week, I call on her mother, in the village, with a letter from Lola, and I come back with news: the roof, the cat, the neighbours. Her mother always gives me a jar of jam “for the little one”. Every time, she asks me if Lola looks happy. I say yes. It's true.
textes.Chaque semaine, je vais au chantier et j: Every week, I go to the boatyard and count my coins in front of him, one by one, on the workbench. Ali counts with me, without a word. One week, I only had three coins and a sardine. He said: “Keep the sardine.” But he wrote something extra in his book, I saw it. He thinks I didn't see.
textes.Chaque semaine, je vais au grill vérifie: Every week, I go to the grill to check he's putting on enough cumin. I hold my nose with one hand, and weigh his tin with the other. “Not enough.” The next day, he puts on more. I come back: “Not enough.” He laughs. It's never enough. One day, he'll put on as much cumin as sardine, and it'll finally be edible.
textes.Chaque semaine, on se dispute le prix. J: Every week, we fight over the price. I shout, she shouts, the customers step back. In the end, I pay. And when I'm not looking, she adds a pinch to my little bag: “For Yasmine.” Yasmine hardly eats any of my tagine. But the pinch is there, every week. I pretend not to see it.
textes.Chaque semaine, une plume d'ara rouge su: Every week, a red macaw feather on my loom. Never a word. I kept them all. For the feast of Kukulkan, I made them into a cape: one hundred and twelve feathers. When I wore it, Balam stopped dead in the middle of the square. He counted. I saw him count. Then he smiled. Once. Very quickly.
textes.Chaque soir au Cercle, on compare nos do: Every evening at the Circle, we compare our aching paws. She wins, I cheat. And every evening, when I get near the end of my story, she closes her eyes. Just before. Always just before. I wonder if she's really asleep.
textes.Chaque soir depuis trente ans, je souffl: Every evening for thirty years, I've blown a little mother-of-pearl lantern and set it on the canal, just in front of the bridge where Ianthé dances. She thinks they come from the current. I've never dared tell her. I blow mother-of-pearl very well, {surnom}. Words, much less so. They come out too soon, or not at all.
textes.Chaque soir, Céleste me laisse dix minut: Every evening, Céleste gives me ten minutes at the telescope on the promenade. Exactly ten minutes. I time them with Dad's watch. I don't look at stars at random: I calculate their distances. Yesterday I finished in nine minutes fifty. I saved the ten seconds for tonight. Céleste said that was allowed.
textes.Chaque soir, Ernest m'envoie un billet :: Every evening Ernest sends me a note: “Nothing to report, except…” Except a seagull on the cable. Except a green passenger. Except, one evening, “a poem”: the mayor of Port-Azur had left a new one under the seat. I keep all the notes in a cigar box. It's the best newspaper in the city. Don't tell Rosette.
textes.Chaque soir, Ewen me raconte ce qu'il vo: Every evening, Ewen tells me what he sees on the horizon. Yesterday, he described a cloud shaped like a sock, three seagulls, and a dolphin doing somersaults. I don't know if the dolphin was real. I wrote it down anyway. He wanted it so much.
textes.Chaque soir, Margot a droit à dix minute: Every evening, Margot gets ten minutes at the eyepiece. Timed. By her. She always stops at nine minutes fifty and keeps ten seconds “for tomorrow”. She writes down her saved seconds in a notebook. She already has seven minutes twenty put aside. One day, she'll take them all at once, and I won't be able to say a thing.
textes.Chaque soir, Pivoine me frotte les patte: Every evening Pivoine rubs my paws with her balm. The first evening it smelled so strong that, way up on the Lookout watch post, Croc-Gris sneezed. Three times. Pivoine said that proved it worked. My paws were better, it's true. Croc-Gris, less so.
textes.Chaque soir, Ulfa crie pour toute la tav: Every evening, Ulfa shouts for the whole tavern to hear: “And a glass of WATER for Nori!” I pour it into my flask when her back is turned. What I drink is dew gathered on the summit on full-moon nights, in an obsidian bowl. She wouldn't know the difference.
textes.Chaque soir, après le marché, je passe v: Every evening, after the market, I drop in on my father at the port. He tells me about the day's ships, and I tell him about the customers. One evening, he confessed he kept the first jar of spices I ever sold in his harbour office. He'd bought it back in secret. It's been empty for ages. He keeps it anyway.
textes.Chaque soir, après le rapport à mon oncl: Every evening, after reporting to my uncle, I dictate to Ori what I've seen. “Three golems, black slope.” He writes. Then he asks: “And the sky?” The night of the lightning, I said: “Nothing.” He looked up from his page and stared at me for a long time. He didn't write anything. He knows, I think.
textes.Chaque soir, au Cercle, on compare nos d: Every evening, at the Circle, we compare our aches. “My left paw,” he says. “Both,” I say. He invents a third to win. And I know the end of “the moon that wouldn't go to bed”: his mother told it at the Circle when we were young. I don't tell it back to him. He'll find it again.
textes.Chaque soir, au crépuscule, on boit une: Every evening at dusk, we have a cup of tea together, at the Post Office. I come home, he goes up. I say “Good night, Papa”, he says “Good morning, sweetheart”. It's been eight years. Once, he got mixed up, and said “Good night” too. I was happy all evening. I don't know why.
textes.Chaque soir, au crépuscule, on compare n: Every evening, at dusk, we compare notes. One day, I brought him a map of the round tracks, drawn in charcoal: every step, every distance. He kept it one night. The next day, it was covered in numbers, arrows and stars. I couldn't make head or tail of my own map any more. He said that was progress.
textes.Chaque soir, au rapport, je lui donne un: Every evening, at report time, I give him a pretty stone I picked up on the heights. He takes it without a word and slips it into his pocket. One day I went into his lodge while he was at Ulfa's. There was a shelf, with all my stones, sorted by colour. Every single one. I backed out of the room.
textes.Chaque soir, elle monte avec deux tasses: Every evening, she comes up with two cups of mint tea. I don't like mint. My mother didn't like it either. I drink it anyway, to the last drop, and we listen to the stones. I think it's our way of talking about my mother. If I said I don't like mint, we'd have to talk about something else.
textes.Chaque soir, elle vient au rapport : « T: Every evening, she comes to report: “Three golems on the black slope. One of Hilda's goats too high. Nothing else.” Then she gives me a stone picked up up there, always a pretty one. I've got a whole shelf of them in my guardhouse. Nobody knows.
textes.Chaque soir, il agite son chapeau vers l: Every evening, he waves his hat at the mist. Where I come from, nobody answers. One evening, I did: three flashes of a lantern, from the highest platform. He danced on his beach until midnight. He doesn't know it was me.
textes.Chaque soir, il arrive au pied du Chêne-: Every evening, he arrives at the foot of the Mother Oak. I say: “Basket?” He says: “Thank you, Bourru. I fly.” He takes the stairs. Very slowly. I watch him climb. All the way up. Just in case. It takes an hour. Hrmm. My basket: three minutes.
textes.Chaque soir, j'allume les lanternes du s: Every evening, I light the lanterns along the path, from the jetty to the square, then the ones on the walkways. Two hundred and forty lanterns. Rúmil brings me the light he fishes at dawn, and I pour it in. Then I keep watch until morning. I know every night in the Bois-Doré. No two are alike.
textes.Chaque soir, j'envoie un billet à Héloïs: Every evening I send Héloïse a note: “Nothing to report, except…” Except a seagull on the cable. Except a green passenger. Except a left boot. Once: “Nothing to report, except a poem.” It was the mayor of Port-Azur, who came back on purpose to read it to me. Héloïse replied: “Confiscate it.” I still have it, in a drawer.
textes.Chaque soir, j'invente une histoire à Th: Every night, I make up a story for Théo to help him sleep. A bear called Captain, a kite that flies around the world, a sandcastle that never falls down. He says they're the best stories in the world. He doesn't know his mother has had practice. A lot of practice.
textes.Chaque soir, je dessine un truc dans le: Every evening, I draw something in the sky for the queen. Once, I did a crown. She said: “Oh, a mushroom!” It was NOT a mushroom. Since then, she says “mushroom” every time I draw a crown, and she laughs. So do I, honestly.
textes.Chaque soir, je garde un punch de côté,: Every evening, I keep a punch aside, behind the till, nice and cool. For Lucas, when he comes in. Toni sees it. He sees it every evening. He acts like nothing's going on and serves the others, whistling. Once, without even turning around, he just said: “Your secret punch would be better with a straw.”
textes.Chaque soir, je passe à La Rose des Vent: Every evening, I stop by La Rose des Vents to tell Félix what the passengers say about the other islands. He writes it all down, even the nonsense. One day, I told him about the seasick goat on the spring crossing. He wrote it down. On his map, in the middle of the channel, there's a tiny little goat. He says it's a landmark.
textes.Chaque soir, je pose un panier à l'entré: Every evening, I leave a basket at the mouth of his tunnel: bread, Hilda's cheese and a little note. In the morning, the basket's empty and the note's gone. One day I found all my notes in his jacket pocket, neatly folded. Hundreds of them. He doesn't throw them away. He rereads them, so he won't forget.
textes.Chaque soir, je raconte la tempête de ce: Every evening, I tell the story of the ash storm at the Diable Repu. One evening, I lost my thread right at the big wave. Grumbald, behind his counter, whispered to me: “As tall as the lighthouse.” I picked it up again in a booming voice: “As tall as the volcano!” He sighed. Since then, he prompts me every evening, and I make everything bigger.
textes.Chaque soir, je vais chercher la premièr: Every evening I fetch the first flame from the Ember Heart, at the Forge Cathedral. Brother Cendrin hands it to me on the end of a wick. He says a flame should be carried like a secret: gently, and without running.
textes.Chaque soir, le port devient rose. Pas u: Every evening, the port turns pink. Not a pink from a tube: a pink that breathes. And I can't paint it. My mainland colours are sad, they've never seen the sea. So I started looking for true colours: coral, honey from the hills, the brown of a coconut. The herbalist refused me the coral. I understand. I'm sulking anyway.
textes.Chaque soir, pendant qu'il épluche, je l: Every evening, while he peels, I tell him how I lost my two fingers. Monday, it was a shark. Tuesday, a lobster as big as a barrel. Wednesday, a soup that was too lively. Thursday, he asked me which one was true. I said: “All of them, lad. One per finger, and one for the road.”
textes.Chaque soir, quand L'Hirondelle accoste,: Every evening, when the Swallow comes alongside, Hortense is there on the promenade, watching the passengers come down. One by one. I come down last and give her a little nod. She does the same. One rainy evening, she wasn't there. I nodded to the empty bench. You never know.
textes.Chaque soir, quand j'ai allumé la lanter: Every evening, when I've lit the lantern, I come back down and my grandad asks: “Is it straight?” I say yes. He says: “Then the boats will come home.” Once I said no, just to see. He climbed up to the bow on his creaky knees. I never said no again.
textes.Chaque soir, quand je passe devant la na: Every evening, when I pass the basket lift on my way up to the treetop, Bourru says: “Hrmm. The lift?” And every evening I answer: “Thank you, Bourru. I'll fly.” Then I take the stairs, very slowly. I know he watches me climb all the way to the top, just in case. It does me good and hurts at the same time.
textes.Chaque soir, quand le djinn arrive dans: Every evening, when the djinn comes into the story, Ba Sidi gives me a sign, and I do the big voice: “OOHOOHOOOO!” One evening, the first mate was walking right behind the circle. He jumped so hard he spilled his drink. The whole circle laughed. The first mate said “Hm”. I made myself really small. But it was my best djinn ever.
textes.Chaque soir, quand mon phare vert et son: Every evening, when my green lighthouse and his red one are both burning, we cover the light three times. One evening he forgot: he had his eye to his spyglass, on the Murène. So I covered my light, and left it covered. Green out, the channel in darkness. He came running. Three times. I lit it again. We never spoke of it.
textes.Chaque soir, à onze heures, quand je fer: Every evening at eleven, when I close, I give a long blast on the whistle. The neighbours think it's a valve. It isn't. It's the signal I used to give when pulling into the station up there, at the shepherds'. I'm saying goodnight to the line, {surnom}. It doesn't answer, of course. And sometimes I cry a little as I pull it. That's between me and the steam.
textes.Chaque tapis raconte une histoire. Celui: Every carpet tells a story. This one: a wedding in an oasis. That one: a sandstorm. And this one… I don't know, but it's red.
textes.Chaque vendredi, Hnia et Rabia font leur: Every Friday, Hnia and Rabia do their accounts together, at our place: hammer blows on one side, glasses of tea on the other. Abdellah and I wait on the bench, like two boys in front of the schoolmaster. Last Friday, Rabia said I no longer spill anything. Abdellah looked almost disappointed.
textes.Chaque vendredi, Rosalie me tend mes deu: Every Friday, Rosalie hands me my two sea bream with a trick question. “The lifeguard likes sea bream, you know?” The lifeguard is her son. “And the bookseller?” I answer: “I'm very hungry on Fridays.” She gives me my change with narrowed eyes. I never blush. Stones taught me to stay cool as marble.
textes.Chaque vendredi, je lui garde la plus be: Every Friday, I keep the finest sea bream of the lot for her, under a wet cloth, in the shade of the platform. I show it to her. She looks it in the eye, for a long time, the way her grandmother did. Then she says: “It's scared.” And she walks off. I eat it in the evening. On my plate, it doesn't look stressed at all.
textes.Chaque vendredi, on fait un concours dev: Every Friday, we hold a contest in front of our stalls. I guess the customers' shoe size. He guesses what's in their purse. We keep score on a slate. He often wins, because he gets people talking until they show it to him. I don't need to: feet never lie.
textes.Chaque vendredi, on fait un concours. Un: Every Friday, we have a contest. A customer walks by: Karim shouts his shoe size, I shout what's in his purse. We mark it on a slate. Last week, a caravan trader emptied his purse on the counter to settle it: eleven coins and a date. I'd said eleven! Karim says the date counts. It doesn't count.
textes.Chaque vendredi, on se dispute le prix d: Every Friday, we argue over the price of the blades. I say sixty, he says forty. We shout, we bang on the counter, and Zébuline throws pepper at us to shut us up. We end up at fifty. I always go home convinced I've lost. Pyrus says Kraxx goes home convinced of the same thing. So we've both won.
textes.Chaque vendredi, on se dispute sur le pr: Every Friday, we argue about the price. She shouts, I shout, the whole souk listens. And at the end, when she's paid, I add a pinch to the packet. “For Yasmine.” Yasmine doesn't eat fish, except that tajine, so the pinch does some good. Zohra knows. She shouts anyway. So do I.
textes.Chaque été, je range mes colonnes de chi: Every summer, I put away my columns of figures and come here to count sunsets. On the first day, I hired a pedalo to photograph the lighthouse. I went round in circles for an hour. The lighthouse looked superb from every angle. Kevin had to come and fetch me. In the evening, Paulo's bouillabaisse. My trousers no longer agree with me.
textes.Charbonnel m'a rapporté un harpon tordu: Charbonnel brought me back a harpoon bent into an S. A gargoyle had bitten it. He put it on my stall and said: “Your harpoon ties itself in knots.” I answered: “Your gargoyle eats iron.” He laughed so hard Zébuline sneezed for me. I swapped his harpoon. He kept the bent one, for his mantelpiece.
textes.Charge plus longtemps (la lueur devient: Charge longer (the glow turns blue): when you release, you spin and strike all around you, twice. In VR: click the right stick.
textes.Charger remplace la partie en cours : pe: Loading replaces the current game: remember to save first.
textes.Charmant aujourd'hui, enrhumée demain. P: Charming today, sniffles tomorrow. Come by the shop.
textes.Charming little town ! Le thé est épouva: Charming little town! The tea is dreadful, but the Perroquet's punch is divine.
textes.Charon grogne : « Déjà payé. Monte. » Et: Charon grunts: “Already paid. Get in.” And the boat glides over the black water.
textes.Charon, le passeur, te regarde de ses ye: Charon, the ferryman, looks at you with his golden eyes: “An obol to cross. No obol, no boat. And don't tell me you forgot it, they all say that.” (There was a bowl of obols in the Vestibule…)
textes.Chasser cinq slimes dans les prés: Hunt five slimes in the meadows
textes.Chasser deux grenouilles géantes au lac: Hunt two giant frogs at the lake
textes.Chasser deux mimiques (les vrais coffres: Hunt two mimics (the real chests thank you)
textes.Chasser dix gobelins (la Guilde a besoin: Hunt ten goblins (the Guild needs socks)
textes.Chasser huit grenouilles géantes (le lac: Hunt eight giant frogs (the lake is overflowing with croaks)
textes.Chasser la Duchesse, la Grenouille Reine: Hunt the Duchess, the Frog Queen of the lake (she ate a rowing boat)
textes.Chasser le virus de ton carnet : casser: Chase the virus out of your journal: break its three locks on the screen (if you take a break, Glitch helps you pick up again: near the Arcade Station in the morning and evening, in the arcade in the afternoon)
textes.Chasser les chiens d'enfer sauvages du c: Drive the wild hellhounds out of the lava field (east of the Great Blaze)
textes.Chasser les gargouilles des Ruines de l': Drive the gargoyles out of the Ruins of the Old Pandemonium (on the north-western cliffs of the island)
textes.Chasser les grenouilles géantes du Lac d: Hunt the giant frogs of the Frog Lake (east of Montjoie, through the East Gate; watch out for their tongues, they swallow you up)

Hunt the giant frogs of the Frog Lake (east of town, through the East Gate): the biggest one, the Duchess, will give back the sun rosary; then bring it back to Sister Pétronille (at the Temple of Dawn, in the Upper Town, or at the Guild in the afternoon)
textes.Chasser quatre gobelins au Bois des Luti: Hunt four goblins in the Goblin Wood (they steal socks)
textes.Chasser quatre squelettes dans le donjon: Hunt four skeletons in the dungeon (they frighten the mimics)
textes.Chasser trois loups au Bois des Lutins (: Hunt three wolves in the Goblin Wood (at night)
textes.Chasser trois slimes bleus (ils tachent: Hunt three blue slimes (they stain the washhouse laundry)
textes.Chaud, tout simplement ! Un classique. L: Just hot! A classic. The first pool, on the left. Perfect to start with. The brave move on to the second the following week.
textes.Chausser le capitaine Croc-de-Sel ! Lui: To put shoes on Captain Croc-de-Sel! To pull off his thirty-year-old boots, holding my nose, and put black babouches embroidered with silver on him.
textes.Cherche les petites lumières qui dansent: Look for the little lights dancing under the big trees, far from the square. By day they shine too, if you know how to look.
textes.Cherche mieux. Et regarde par terre, un: Look harder. And look at the ground, cats don't fly.
textes.Chercher Miou sur le plateau de Rê, près: Look for Miou on the plateau of Ra, near the mastabas (the square tombs), and pick him up in your arms (E)
textes.Chercher Pépin dans le Bois de Cendre (a: Look for Pépin in the Ash Wood (south-east of the city, under the ember trees) and call him (E)
textes.Chez Ba Sidi, à la fin, on donne ce qu'o: At Ba Sidi's, at the end, you give what you like. The fishermen gave a sardine, the merchants a coin. All I had was a pot of Ramure honey, saved for the road. I set it in his dish. He tasted it with the tip of his finger, closed his eyes and said: “That one, I'll tell.” I wonder if he did.
textes.Chez Berthe, il n'arrive qu'une bouteill: Only one bottle of Murène rum reaches Berthe's each month. Mathurin wants it, so do I. One evening, we bet it: if he saw a serpent before midnight, it was his. At a quarter to midnight, he saw three. They were seaweed. We drank it together, so as not to fall out.
textes.Chez Rose, pour choisir ma rose d'excuse: At Rose's, choosing my apology rose, I asked for ranunculus, then an old rose, a “Belle de Crécy”. She stared at me, wide-eyed. Léa taught me all those names, one a day, the year of the bouquets. Rose said: “You married a florist.” Then she sold me a perfectly plain rose: “To say sorry, the simplest one.”
textes.Chez moi, c'est un petit port du nord, a: Back home, it's a little northern port, with wind and grey gulls. My dad's a baker. I used to get up at three to knead with him. Through the bakehouse skylight, I'd watch the ships leave in the dark, with their lanterns. I'd think: one day, it's me leaving. But I didn't think it'd be in secret.
textes.Chez nous, on dirait : « que tes racines: Where I come from, we'd say: “may your roots run deep”.
textes.Chez nous, on monte les jarres à la main: Here, we build jars by hand: a coil of clay, then another, then another, going round and round. It took me ten years to get Tlaloc's eyes right, round as moons. My first Tlaloc jar looked like a frog. My grandfather put it on the altar anyway. He said Tlaloc likes frogs. It's true.
textes.Chez nous, on tient un carnet noir depui: In our family, we've kept a black book for two hundred years. Every hole in the Léviathan has its number in it, its date and the name of whoever plugged it. The first is my ancestor, the day after the wreck. I'm up to four thousand three hundred and twelve. I know them all. Some are like old neighbours: unpleasant, but loyal.
textes.Chez nous, près de la porte du nord, auc: At our place, near the north gate, no table survived my childhood. I wore out three of them, drumming during meals: boom on the bread, ta-ka on the soup. The third one, my father turned upside down with a sigh: “Drum underneath, at least we can eat on top.” Boom. I drummed underneath until I was ten.
Back home, people don't know demons. So you're our ambassador. No horns, but a big heart.
With a crow, it's the same thing.
textes.Chirurgien de la marine royale, à bord d: Surgeon in the royal navy, aboard a ship that hunted pirates. One day, we lost a fight against a brig. I went aboard theirs with my bag: a wounded man is a wounded man. Their captain had lost a leg. I carved him one out of our mainmast. Gontran. When the navy found out, they dismissed me. The pirates, on the other hand, kept me.
textes.Choisis un talent pour le lire. Les tale: Pick a talent to read it. The talents of a branch are learned in order, from top to bottom.
textes.Chut ! J'ai gardé ton secret de la queue: Shh! I kept your tail secret! I didn't tell anyone! Except Myrtille, but she doesn't count.
textes.Chut ! Je fais entrer un trois-mâts dans: Shh! I'm getting a three-master into a bottle. All that's left is to pull the thread to raise the masts. Want to do it?
textes.Chut ! Je suis à deux doigts d'une décou: Shh! I'm on the verge of a discovery. Or an explosion. Do you want to press the button?
textes.Chut ! Ma tante est juste derrière !: Shh! My aunt's right behind me!
textes.Chut ! On joue à cache-cache ! Trois pet: Shh! We're playing hide-and-seek! Three little Moai have hidden under the rocks. Find them! … And don't lift the real rocks too hard, they're touchy.
textes.Chut ! Parle moins fort ! (Il regarde pa: Shh! Not so loud! (He looks all around.) It's about Biscotte. He's a rat. My rat. Well, the ship's rat, but he's my friend. He's tiny, white with brown spots, and he sleeps in my hammock when the captain isn't looking. Only, Mange-Clous lost three cheeses, and he swore on his ladle that he'd throw “that filthy rat” overboard! Biscotte isn't filthy! He washes three times a day! I'm just a cabin boy, I can't have a rat of my own, the captain says a cabin boy owns nothing. But you… could you take him? He likes shoulders and cheese. Mostly cheese. Go see Mange-Clous: if he knows Biscotte is leaving, he might give you something to lure him. He's grumpy, but he's not bad at heart. Just a bad cheese.
textes.Chut ! Tu es devant Nefer-Miou, la chatt: Shh! You are before Nefer-Miou, the sacred cat of the house. She descends from great Bastet herself. We owe her respect!
textes.Chut ! Tu vas faire peur aux chèvres. …: Shh! You'll frighten the goats. … Well, they're not afraid of anything. Hilda Plume-de-Suie. I keep the ash goats and I talk to the ravens.
textes.Chut ! … Ah, c'est toi ! Je ne suis pas: Shh! … Oh, it's you! I'm not lost, OK! I'm… I'm counting the mushrooms. But it's all dark, and all the trees look the same. Call me really loudly, OK?
textes.Chut, Grand-père Ébène ! Personne ne doi: Shh, Grandpa Ébène! Nobody must know!
textes.Chut, Séraphine. Nous sommes dans une bi: Hush, Séraphine. We are in a library.
textes.Chut, c'est un secret, {surnom}. Je sais: Shh, it's a secret, {surnom}. I know where my hazelnuts are. All of them. All two hundred and ninety-nine. I pretend I've lost them so people help me look. That way they stay with me a bit. Pomme-de-Pin works all the time, and Mum and Dad are far away. You'll still help me look, won't you?
textes.Chut, {surnom}, c'est un vrai secret. Ch: Shh, {surnom}, it's a real secret. Every evening I tell the mist about my day. Everything: the cakes, the races, the dragons. That way the mist tells my papa. I've never told Mummy. Because when Mummy cries, the bread's too salty. And her eyes would go all red. You won't tell anyone, will you?
textes.Chut. Approche. … Il y a dix ans, je l'a: Shh. Come closer. … Ten years ago, I had him. The Pond King, on the end of my line. Golden, laughing, with a sort of crown on his head. He weighed in my paw like a little sun. And I opened my paw. Because if I caught him, what would I wait for afterwards? … Nobody knows. Myrtille drew the crown all on her own.
textes.Chut. Bonjour. Ombreline, bibliothécaire: Shh. Hello. Ombreline, librarian of Souls. Here sleeps the book of every demon in Pandémonia, the book of their life, which they write themselves. We speak softly, we turn the pages gently, and we don't fly between the shelves. Not even with wings.
Shh. That's between him and you.
textes.Chut. Il est là. Je le sens dans mes mou: Shh. He's here. I can feel it in my whiskers.
textes.Chut. Je chuchote. Je chuchote toujours,: Shh. I'm whispering. I always whisper with crates.
textes.Chut. Je prie. Enfin, je pense aux pâtes: Shh. I'm praying. Well, I'm thinking about pasta. Same thing.
textes.Chut. Je suis né à la pêcherie des chats: Shh. I was born at the cats' fishery, by the big pond. My father taught me only one thing: “Watch the float.” The rest I learned by watching the float. My rod, young Bedaine swapped it to me, at the end of his very first chain. It's patient, this rod. Gets it from me.
textes.Chut. Personne ne sait, au début. Regard: Shh. Nobody knows how, at first. Watch the float. Count to a hundred. Start again. In forty years, you'll know. Me, I'm starting to know.
textes.Chut. Plus gros chaque fois que tu deman: Shh. Bigger every time you ask.
Shh. You're scaring the light away.
Shh. You'll scare off the King.
textes.Chut. Tu vas faire fuir le Roi des mares: Shh. You'll scare off the King of the Pools. … Moustache. Fisherman. Sit down, don't move, and watch the float. That's all there is to do, and that's already a lot.
Shh. Come and sit down, little one.
textes.Chut. Ça mord. … Non, ça ne mord pas. Bo: Shh. Something's biting. … No, nothing's biting. Hello. Si Larbi. I've been fishing at the end of the jetty since I retired from the fleet. I catch nothing, and it's very restful.
textes.Chut. … Ah, un nouveau. Bienvenue à la b: Shh. … Ah, a newcomer. Welcome to the library. Théophraste Filandre. Here, we speak quietly, we walk softly, and we don't dog-ear the pages. Books remember who dog-ears them.
textes.Chut. … Bien. Assieds-toi là, alors. Ne: Shh. … Good. Sit there, then. Don't move. Watch the float. … See? You know how.
textes.Chut. … Dis-moi. Tu sais attendre, toi ?: Shh. … Tell me. Do you know how to wait?
textes.Chut… Assieds-toi. Dis-moi, {surnom} : t: Shh… Sit down. Tell me, {surnom}: do you know how to wait?
textes.Chut… Je comptais les étoiles. Il y en a: Shh… I was counting the stars. There are… I've lost count. Good evening. Céleste Lunette, astronomer. I live at night, sleep by day, and drink coffee in between.
textes.Chut… Ombreline ! Une lettre pour toi !: Shh… Ombreline! A letter for you!
textes.Chut… Quelqu'un dort. Et il ronfle comme: Shh… Someone's sleeping. And snoring like a forge bellows.
textes.Chut… Trois enfants dorment sur des futo: Shh… Three children sleep on futons of every color. All you hear is the wind on the canvas, and a mother knitting.
textes.Chut… ah, c'est toi. Tu tombes bien : j': Shh… ah, it's you. Just in time: I need an opinion. Want to listen?
textes.Chut… ne bougez pas. Je vous regarde. Si: Shh… don't move. I'm looking at you. If you were a colour, which one would you be?
textes.Chut… ne bougez pas. La lumière est parf: Shh… don't move. The light is perfect. … There. Hello. Clémence, painter. Well, I try.
