may none ever bring them together."
textes.« Il range ton sac, il trouve les trésor: “It tidies your bag, finds the treasures, even does your homework.” — Mr. Fil
textes.« Ils sont cachés ! Trouve-les ! » chuch: “They're hiding! Find them!” whispers a little Moai. The rocks hold their breath.
textes.« J'ai beaucoup d'or, et de beaux habits: “I have lots of gold and fine clothes.”
textes.« Je n'ai pas menti, je n'ai pas volé, j: “I have not lied, I have not stolen, I have made no one cry.”
textes.« Je suis caché ! Cherche-moi ! » dit un: “I'm hidden! Come find me!” says a child's voice. The room is messy: there are hiding places everywhere.
textes.« Je suis le plus fort : j'ai vaincu tou: “I am the strongest: I have defeated all my enemies.”
textes.« Journal du capitaine Bourrache, jour 1: “Journal of Captain Bourrache, day 1: I buy this house. Day 2: a leak in the ceiling. Day 3: two leaks. Day 4: I'm going back to sea. It's drier.”
textes.« L'eau qui regarde le ciel »… le lac du: “The water that looks at the sky”… the crater lake?
textes.« L'homme. » Bébé, il marche à quatre pa: “Man.” As a baby, he crawls on all fours; grown, he walks on his two legs; old, with a stick. Good.
textes.« LISSE & FILS — Plan des étages. -1 : l: “LISSE & SONS — Floor plan. -1: the Offices. -2: the Assembly Line. -3: the Boiler Room. -4: the Automated Warehouse. -5: the President's Pit (no entry, especially for you).” Someone has added in marker pen: “and all the way down: the machine that wants to flatten Boucan”.
textes.« La Marguerite », « Vague 1 » à « Vague: “La Marguerite”, “Vague 1” to “Vague 6”, “Gérard” and… “Gertrude”? Well. It's noted. Thank you, really. Here, for your trouble.
textes.« La flamme brûle, la braise cuit. C'est: “The flame burns, the ember cooks. It's the same with people.” That's my father's. He was a man of flame: always angry, always burning. I chose to be an ember. Gentle, slow, warm. And yet, {surnom}… the fake recipe I gave the pirate cook, that was a bit of flame. I'm ashamed of it. A little. I still laugh, though.
textes.« La la laaaa ! » Cinq petits Moaïs chan: “La la laaaa!” Five little Moai sing in a half circle. Not all the same song.
textes.« La passe des Récifs de Feu est à l'est: “The pass through the Fire Reefs is east of the dwarves' island, facing the rising sun. Follow the map.”
textes.« Larsen ! », la compilation du festival: “Feedback!”, the compilation from the festival twenty years ago
textes.« Le Chant des Quatre Cloches. Qui voudr: “The Song of the Four Bells. Whoever would have the Crystal of the Dawn shall ring the belfry as the Sky Kings sang: the Wave bears the Sun; the Sun chases the Moon; the Moon calls the Wind.” Further down, in another hand: “The Crystal of the Dusk sleeps in the armoury. Its guardians never sleep.”
textes.« Le Puits des Abysses. Ici dort ce que: “The Well of the Abyss. Here sleeps what the Ancients have chained.”
textes.« Le chemin des Anciens suit le chant de:
"The path of the Ancients follows the song of the fresco.
Twice."
“The path of the Ancients follows the song of the fresco. Twice.” Every slab in the lake bears one of the four symbols.
textes.« Le royaume refleurit. Les fées chanten: “The kingdom blooms again. The fairies sing once more. Thank you, human.”
textes.« Le vent t'a vu passer, ici, là-bas, pa: “The wind has seen you pass, here, there, everywhere. The fairies will teach you to do the same.”
textes.« Le visiteur terrasse la bête » ! Votre: “Visitor slays the beast”! Your monster has grown two metres since the first draft. That's the press for you.
textes.« Les Poissons, les troisièmes, dansèren: “The Fish, the third, danced in his shadow to show him the way.”
textes.« Les deux » ?! … Un diplomate. On a un: “Both”?! … A diplomat. We have a DIPLOMAT in the house. … Fine. Here, for the trip. And off with you before we start arguing again.
“Dwarves don't like surprises. Knock hard at their door, but politely.”
textes.« Les quatre fleurs fleuriront quand cha: “The four flowers will bloom when each lives its season. Where the sun is born, all awakens. Where it reigns at noon, all blazes. Where it dies, all sheds its leaves. Where it never goes, all sleeps beneath the snow.” Below: spring, summer, autumn, winter.
textes.« Mille talents ! » grince le poids. (C': “A thousand talents!” creaks the weight. (It's written on it.)
textes.« Mmmm-mmm-mmm… oh. » Quark s'arrête de: “Mmmm-mmm-mmm… oh.” Quark stops humming. “How did you know?” (He never realised he was humming.)
textes.« Non, hmpf » ? Presque la bonne réponse: “No, hmph”? Almost the right answer. I'll note it down.
textes.« Nourrissantes », m'aviez-vous dit. Cor: “Filling”, you told me. Coralin laughed for an hour when I told him. Traitor.
textes.« Nous partons chercher fortune à Astral: “We're off to seek our fortune in Astralys. They say that up there, the streets are paved with crystal. If you're reading this, take what's in the chest: we won't need it anymore. — The Delaunay family”
textes.« Oh non ! Trouvée ! » Pixel sort de sa: “Oh no! Found!” Pixel comes out of her hiding place laughing, her antennae all blinking. “You have telescope eyes!”
textes.« Osiris. » Seth l'a trahi, Isis l'a ras: “Osiris.” Seth betrayed him, Isis gathered him together. Remember it, down below: his body is still scattered.
textes.« PLAN POUR CONQUÉRIR LE MONDE. Étape 1: “PLAN TO CONQUER THE WORLD. Step 1: get up early. Step 2: have a good breakfast. Step 3: … well, we'll see tomorrow.”
“They say you snore like a seal.”
“Gone on vacation. Back soon. — 12 years later: not back yet. Vacations are nice.”
textes.« Pas le temps », {surnom}. C'est ce que: “No time,” {surnom}. That's what I told Madame Hortense for seven years. It was a lie. I was scared. A botched sword still cuts. A botched cog, the clock doesn't ring, and she'd have waited seven years for nothing. For a blacksmith with shaky hands. Hm. Don't repeat that.
textes.« Pas mal, petit ! Mais Gorgoth n'a pas: “Not bad, kid! But Gorgoth hasn't shown his finest horns yet!”
textes.« Pluie d'été », des Gouttières et du Ca: “Summer Rain,” by The Gutters and Flower Camp, recorded at the last Feedback Festival. Spleen plays it when he thinks nobody's looking. He cries a little, every time.
textes.« Plus longue ! » « Plus BELLE ! » Deux: “Longer!” “More BEAUTIFUL!” Two dwarves squabble in front of a mirror.
textes.« Pépin ! » … Une petite voix répond der: “Pépin!” … A tiny voice answers from behind the trunk: “I'm here! I wanted to see the glowing mushrooms… and then it got all dark.” Pépin runs home to his mummy at the Great Market.
textes.« Quand la nuit soulève la mer, le jour:
“When the night lifts the sea, the day rises,
and the guardian awakes.”
textes.« Que les quatre serpents contemplent l':
"May the four serpents behold the Eye.
But no serpent turns alone."
“May the four serpents behold the Eye. But no serpent turns alone.” The channels in the floor lead from each serpent to the altar.
textes.« Qui vient là ? Un vivant ! » Minos, le: “Who comes there? A living one!” Minos, the judge, leans forward, and his serpent tail coils. "Answer three questions about your journey.
textes.« Raconte ta vie, ça va m'endormir. »: “Tell me your life story, it'll put me to sleep.”
textes.« Rrrrr… pfff… » La pièce entière vibre: “Rrrrr… pfff…” The whole room gently vibrates to the rhythm of a stone snore.
“Rules of the Dungeon of a Thousand Steps. 1. Do not feed the slimes (they grow). 2. Do not pet the frogs (they swallow). 3. A chest that smiles is not a chest. 4. The blue crystals bring you back up here. The falls do not.” Signed: Odon, keeper and step counter.
textes.« Rê, le soleil. » Khépri le matin, Rê à: “Ra, the sun.” Khepri in the morning, Ra at noon, Atum in the evening. Every night, I travel in his barque until dawn.
textes.« Salut à toi, Hun-Camé, salut à toi, Vu: “Greetings, Hun-Camé, greetings, Vucub-Camé!” The two great Lords half rise: “So you know us… Enter our Houses, traveller. If you come out again, we shall play ball.” Behind them, the door sinks into the floor.
textes.« Salut à toi, grand Seigneur ! »… Tu as: “Greetings, great Lord!”… You greeted a WOODEN DUMMY. A terrible laugh rolls beneath the vault: all the Lords are mocking you. And from the ceiling, bats come loose!
textes.« Seul passera celui qui écrit le nom du: “Only he shall pass who writes the king's name as Thoth wrote it. The first sign on the left, the last on the right.”
textes.« Tes bras sont chargés, humain… Fais un: “Your arms are full, human… Make a little room in your bag: I have a map, coins and nectar for you.”
textes.« Tes copains, ils sont aussi laids que: “Are your mates as ugly as you?”
“Tlaloc is thirsty”? Then it's serious. (He takes from his kiln a blue jar with big round eyes, dips it in the lake and plugs it with a leaf.) There. Full of lake water, and don't spill it on the way.
textes.« Ton sac est trop plein pour ce que j'a: “Your bag is too full for what I have to give you, little traveller. Make some room.”
textes.« Tout existe déjà »… Vous avez parlé à: “Everything's been invented”… You've been talking to Philibert, haven't you? He rubs off on people. Don't believe him too much: he only half believes it himself. On Mondays, much less.
textes.« Trois bonnes réponses. Tu as bien rega: “Three right answers. You've watched your path well.” Minos sits back down and uncoils his tail. “Pass. The wind blows hard on the other side: shelter behind the pillars.”
textes.« Trois… deux… un… VZIIIOU ! » Comète dé: “Three… two… one… VZIIIOU!” Comète shoots off! Fly through all the rings (the next one glows gold) and get back to the starting ring before she does!
textes.« Tu as l'esprit clair, voyageur. Va : l: “You have a clear mind, traveller. Go: the door of Ra is open. But beware of Apophis, who waits for the barque of the sun at the bottom of the night.”
textes.« Tu l'as vue, toi, la mer ? » demande u: “Have you seen it, the sea?” asks a tiny stone voice.
textes.« Tu les as déjà ! Les chaussettes, ça n: “You already have them! Socks don't wear out if you don't walk in puddles. Do you walk in puddles?”
textes.« Tête de méduse » ?! Ha ha ! Bartholomé: “Jellyfish-head”?! Ha ha! Bartholomé will be jealous! But it's affectionate, eh! Always affectionate!
textes.« UN, DEUX, TROIS : GRIMACE ! » Rien ne: “ONE, TWO, THREE: GRIMACE!” Nothing changes on their stone faces. They look very proud.
textes.« Une trace, c'est une phrase. Plusieurs: “A track is a sentence. Several make a story.” That's how I learned to read, on my knees in the ferns. At ten, first exam: find a mooncake hidden somewhere in the forest. I found it in one morning, under a stump. But Bedaine's tracks were already there. And half the cake had left with them.
textes.« Vous qui entrez ici, gardez l'espoir (: “You who enter here, keep hope (and take a coat).”
textes.« Vous qui entrez ici, laissez toute esp: “Abandon all hope, you who enter here.”
textes.« À qui trouvera ce mot : j'ai caché mes: “To whoever finds this note: I hid my savings in the chest, for my old age. I'm old now. And I forgot where the house was. If you find me, keep everything.”
textes.« Ça dépend des îles », m'as-tu dit. J'a: “Depends on the island”, you told me. I've made a list of our grumblers, just in case. Coralin is on it twice.
“Depends which ones,” you told me. I repeat it at the fishermen's council. Without saying it came from you.
textes.« Ça dépend », vous m'aviez dit. Sauf po: “It depends,” you told me. Except for boots, I hope. Boots, you keep.
textes.« … 98… 99… 100 ! » Quelqu'un fait des p: “… 98… 99… 100!” Someone is doing push-ups in the middle of the living room.
textes.À Cliquetis, ils m'ont troqué une bousso: In Cliquetis, they swapped me a compass that points south. I swapped it in Carène for a telescope that sees the past. I swapped that in Tazira for a carpet that doesn't fly. I've still got it. Nobody wants it.
textes.À Forgefer, il m'écrivait chaque semaine: In Forgefer, he wrote to me every week. Six pages. Stories, news, Mum's honey recipe. I replied once. “Cold. Good. Ursule.” He keeps the letter on him. I see it poking out of his pocket, all folded. Hm. I should have written a fourth word.
textes.À Port-Azur, je peignais la mer et les t: In Port-Azur, I painted the sea and the terraces. Here, everything is stronger: the sun, the colours, the smells, the noise. I'm never leaving.
textes.À Tazira, ils dansent aussi, sur la plac: In Tazira they dance too, in the square, every evening. Roux showed me their steps. It looks like a goat dance. I learned it anyway.
textes.À Tazira, ils ont des musiciens qui joue: In Tazira, they have musicians who play all night in the square. I listened to them from the Zéphyr. I wrote down their rhythms. My piano is going to dance.
textes.À Tazira, ils pêchent en mer, sur de gra: In Tazira, they fish at sea, on big boats. The sea is too much water. A pool is just the right size.
textes.À bientôt ! Si tu as froid, reviens : ic: See you soon! If you're cold, come back: here, there's always an ember for you.
textes.À bientôt, {surnom} ! Que tes oreilles r: See you soon, {surnom}! Keep your ears warm.
See you soon. And don't touch anything that's smoking.
See you soon. Bois-Doré awaits you.
textes.À bientôt. Les dieux regardent, alors ma: See you soon. The gods are watching, so walk straight.
textes.À bientôt. Marche doucement : il y a des: See you soon. Walk softly: there are flowers everywhere.
All aboard! Left stick to sail.
textes.À bord ! Z / S pour avancer, Q / D pour: All aboard! W / S to move forward, A / D to steer.
textes.À bras ouverts… Tu le dis avec tant de c: With open arms… You say it with such certainty. Perhaps I'm the one who has forgotten how to open her arms. A thousand years under a dome stiffens the shoulders.
textes.À cent ans, Thalion m'a pris comme éclai: At a hundred, Thalion took me on as a scout. He taught me to walk without a sound, to read moss, to count my steps in the mist. For two centuries I've given him my report every evening. He says “good”. Only once did he say “good work”. That was the day I brought Elandor back.
textes.À cent ans, j'ai hérité des jardins et d: At a hundred, I inherited the gardens and my father's rule: one seaweed in three, no more. The day Thalassa cut mine without asking, I scolded her. She came back with a scarf. I still don't know how that ended in marriage. But I still have the scarf.
textes.À cent ans, je suis entré en apprentissa: At a hundred, I was apprenticed to Coralin. Three hundred years of cutting mother-of-pearl, sweeping the workshop, saying “yes, master”. I learned a lot. Above all, never to touch red coral: I've still got the bite mark, here, on my thumb. Pff… I'm rather fond of that mark.
textes.À cette heure-ci, je pense surtout au re: At this time of day, all I think about is lunch.
textes.À chaque Foire, Ambroise passe devant mo: At every Fair, Ambroise walks past my stand without looking at the engine. Never. He looks at his shoes, he looks at the sky, he looks at Capucine's cannon. Not the engine. The day the gear fell, he probably didn't even look up from his chessboard. He must have read about it in the Gazette, like everyone else.
textes.À chaque fin d'année, je lui laisse un p: At the end of every year, I leave her a jar of honey on the counter. The best one, from the hills. Without a word. Free. Yes, free. She says it's the only present I've ever given. It isn't a present. It's for her silence. Silence needs looking after.
textes.À chaque fête de la Forge, je lève ma ch: At every Forge Festival, I raise my mug to him and shout: “No hard feelings, Bramm!” He never raises his. But last year, Ulfa whispered to me that he'd taken a sip, just as I was shouting. One sip. It's a start.
textes.À chaque fête de la Forge, la garde de l: At every Forge Festival, the hall guard challenges the gate guard to arm-wrestling. Gunnar challenges me every year. He loses every year. Last year, he held out for eleven seconds. That's better than before. I didn't tell him.
textes.À chaque tempête qu'on traverse, elle fa: For every storm we go through, she cuts a notch in my wooden leg, with the tip of a knife. Eleven notches. I pretend to get angry. She says one day there'll be no room left, and they'll have to carve me a second one. Hm. There won't be a second one.
textes.À chaque tempête traversée, je fais une: For every storm we come through, I cut a notch in his wooden leg with my smallest knife. There are eleven. The first time, he howled. The second, he grumbled. Now, after every storm, he comes and sits on the crate next to me and holds out his leg, without a word, looking the other way.
textes.À chaque élection, il entre dans l'isolo: At every election, he goes into the voting booth shouting “Thief!” and comes out shouting “Thief!”. At the count, there's always a ballot for me with a little flour on it: forty years of baking, it doesn't come out of your pockets. I've never said anything. He thinks it's a secret.
textes.À chaque élection, je lui apporte une po: At every election, I bring her an apple. The finest at the market, polished on my sleeve. She weighs it and refuses it. Last time, she'd worked out the interest since I was ten: four hundred and twelve coins and change. I offered to pay in two instalments. She said: “No credit for mayors.”
textes.À chaque élection, je vote pour Aristide: At every election, I vote for Aristide. I slip my ballot into the box shouting “Thief!” so everyone can hear. The mayor shakes my hand on the way out: “Thank you, my dear Raymond.” And every year he offers me a rematch, and every year he loses it. On purpose, I think. That's even more annoying.
textes.À cinq ans, Frère Cendrin m'a donné une: When I was five, Brother Cendrin gave me a candle lit at the Heart-Brazier. He told me: “Keep it, and you'll never be cold.” It's still burning, in my bedroom, on the mantelpiece. I look at it every night before I go to sleep. Such a tiny flame, and it keeps a whole Archduchess warm.
textes.À cinq ans, Vespérine a étiqueté tous me: At five, Vespérine labelled all my jam jars, with the date, the weight and the fruit's scientific name. I opened the cupboard, read it all, and looked at her for a long time. She looked so serious, with her pencil behind her horn. I told her: “You take after your father.” He labelled everything too. Even our wedding cake.
textes.À cinq ans, elle a voulu tisser comme mo: At five, she wanted to weave like me. She sat at the loom while I was selling at the stall. When I came back, she had woven herself in, her sleeve caught in the warp, and she was singing while she waited. It took me an hour to undo her. She told me, very proudly: “I'm a dress.”
textes.À cinq ans, j'ai étiqueté tous les pots: At five, I labelled all my mother's jam jars, with the date, the weight and the scientific name of the fruit. She opened the cupboard, she read, she closed the cupboard. Then she looked at me for a long time and said: “You take after your father.” I never knew if it was a compliment. I recorded it as one.
At two hundred, I took over the south bridge. It's the best of the four: you can see the square, the crystal and a bit of Gate Avenue. In the evening I dance the tide with seaweed ribbons, and the children follow me from bridge to bridge, all the way round the canal. They say that's going round the world. I've never checked.
textes.À deux cents ans, une tempête a cassé un: When I was two hundred, a storm broke a branch off the Mother Tree. We never cut the Tree. But what falls, we may keep. I spent a year carving my bow from that branch. My father tried it. He said: “It's better than mine.” He gave it back. I became a guard the next day.
About becoming a tree. That takes time.
textes.À dix ans, elle a troqué un panier de po: At ten, she swapped a basket of apples for a goat. My heart sang: a true tanuki! Then the goat ate the rest of the apples. And the basket. My niece looked at the goat, then at me, and said: “From now on, I want coins.” I had to sit down. I never really got back up.
textes.À dix ans, j'ai trouvé un livre de sorci: At ten, I found a wizard's book at the Inventions Fair, on a stall of old papers. The first page talked about Arcanelle. I read the whole book that night. In the morning, my parents found me sitting on my bed, my suitcase packed. They cried a little. So did I. But not for long. They sent me to the archmage.
textes.À dix ans, j'ai vendu la marmite de ma m: At ten, I sold my mother's cooking pot to a passer-by, very dear. My mother had to buy it back from him for twice as much. She punished me for a week. My father, though, took me aside and whispered: “Good sale. Bad customer.” That day I understood that trade is knowing who to sell to. And who not to sell to: your mother.
textes.À dix ans, je soignais déjà les oiseaux: At ten, I was already caring for the island's injured birds. One day, an old sailor arrived with a grey parrot in a rusty cage. The parrot wouldn't talk any more. I kept him for a week, I whistled songs to him. On the eighth day, he said: “Jellyfish-head!” The sailor cried with joy. He left him with me. That was Bartholomé.
textes.À dix ans, mon premier troc : un panier: At ten, my first swap: a basket of apples for a goat. A fine goat! It ate the rest of the apples, then the basket, then a corner of my apron. That day I understood: coins don't eat anything. Since then, I sell for coins. My uncle never got over it. Neither did the goat: it had a tummy ache.
textes.À dix ans, mon père est revenu du souk a: When I was ten, my father came back from the souk with a bendir, the round goatskin drum. “To save the tables,” he said. I struck it once, and under the skin something buzzed. The snare string! I thought the drum was answering me. I didn't sleep all night. Neither did the neighbours. The next day they applauded me. Out of exhaustion, I think.
textes.À dix heures, la flotte rentre. Les cais: At ten o'clock, the fleet comes in. The crates go up on the quay, I go up on my platform, and I cry out the prices. Whoever raises a hand first takes the lot. You have to be quick. And not have an itchy nose.
textes.À dix-huit ans, Pierrick a peint « AUBER: At eighteen, Pierrick painted “INN” on a plank and nailed it under the tavern sign. He'd forgotten the last N: it said “IN”. I didn't say anything. One morning, the N was there, painted smaller, a bit crooked. Nobody knows who added it. Me, maybe.
textes.À dix-huit ans, Si Larbi m'a pris sur sa: At eighteen, Si Larbi took me on his boat. The first day, he told me one sentence: “Watch the seagulls.” I watched them. In the evening I said: “They come home before us.” He nodded. That's the whole secret. Later, Ali's father built me the Mabrouka. Forty years we've been coming home with the seagulls, she and I.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai décidé que la taver: At eighteen, I decided the tavern and the inn were two different things. I painted “INN” on a plank and nailed it under the sign. I'd forgotten an N. The next day, someone had added it, crooked. I never found out who. Since then, I take care of the hammocks, and my aunt of everything else. It's very different.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai ouvert mon étal au: At eighteen, I opened my stall at the Great Market with three jars: fire cinnamon, ash pepper, sulphur salt. On the first day, I sold just one jar, to a little girl with a hood and horns like a crown. Ignatia. She still comes back, in secret, with Captain Pyrus twenty paces behind her.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai pris mon sac d'outi: At eighteen, I took my bag of tools and left on the first ship that came into the bay. It was the Merciless, a pirate three-master that needed a shipwright. I didn't ask questions. Neither did they. For five years, I repaired her masts, her decks, her hull. I know her plank by plank.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai repris l'étal, le p: At eighteen, I took over the stall, the first in the fish auction, the one everyone sees when they arrive. That same year, a young sailor came to buy a sea bream from me. I looked him in the eye, like grandmother: he wasn't lying. It was Abdelkader. I married him in the spring. The sea bream, he never paid for it. I'm still counting on it.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai traversé jusqu'à la: At eighteen, I crossed over to Fire Mountain. I wanted to forge. Borin gave me a sack of coal. Three years, the coal. Not one hammer. The day he handed me one, I trembled. I came back with a scorched apron and one sentence: “Not bad… for a tall one.” I still have the apron. The sentence too.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai voulu ouvrir une éc: At eighteen, I wanted to open a dance school on the village square. I made a poster, swept the cobbles, waited. Nobody came, except the cat from the little house. He sat down, watched, and came back the next day. So I kept going, for him. He's still there. Never misses a class.
textes.À dix-huit ans, j'ai vu le reflet de la: At eighteen, I saw the moon's reflection move in a pond. I followed it, from pond to pond, eastward, for a whole moon, up to the cliffs above the sea: the edge of the world. There, the moon said to me: “Go home, Ramure needs you.” I only knew Ramure by name. I understood that evening: home is where someone is waiting for you.
textes.À dix-huit ans, on m'a donné la grue. J': At eighteen, they gave me the crane. I soon learned that in Cliquetis, it's not just rain that falls. Boots first, by the dozen. Then the wheel of Gaston's locomotive, the day they hoisted it up there, two fan-hats, and the flywheel of an old engine of Firmin's. What falls belongs to the crane. That's the law of the quay. Well, it's my law.
textes.À dix-huit ans, un touriste s'est retrou: At eighteen, a tourist got stuck under an upturned pedalo, head underwater. I dived, lifted the pedalo with one hand and the gentleman with the other. All right, with both hands. The next day, the mayor gave me a whistle, a high chair and a red swimsuit. I never gave them back.
textes.À dix-neuf ans, je suis monté sur le bat: At nineteen, I got on my cousin Mano's boat, the one that delivers coconuts from the jungle. I got off here with a bag, a machete and no plan. The first few weeks, I was homesick. I ate ice cream at Bruno's kiosk to cheer myself up. One day, I saw his coconut ice cream recipe on the counter. I… borrowed it. Forever.
textes.À dix-sept ans, au grand match de la fêt: At seventeen, in the big match of the Kukulkan festival, I sent the ball through the stone ring. The first in twenty years in Yaxché! Where I come from, whoever does it has the right to take the spectators' cloaks. I ran towards the stands. Everyone fled clutching their cloak. I didn't get a single one. But I had the ring.
textes.À dix-sept ans, je suis parti mousse sur: At seventeen, I went off as a cabin boy on a merchant ship. I saw Port-Azur and its white terraces. An island where the trees touched the sky. And one night, a whale as big as the Skala, which blew so close to us that I got soaked right up to my cap. I was meant to stay four years. I came home after three.
textes.À dix-sept ans, le vieux crieur, Ba Jila: When I was seventeen, the old crier, Ba Jilali, lost his voice one winter morning. Not a sound. Moulay Brahim looked along the quay and said: “The kid who yells. Up he goes.” Up I went. I shouted “SARDIIINES!” and every gull on the Skala took off at once. Since then, the camels at the north gate raise their heads when I announce the sea bream.
textes.À dix-sept ans, mousse sur la barque de: At seventeen, cabin boy on Fernand's boat. On the second day, I was telling a gripping story, I leaned over… and splash. Fernand fished me out with the boathook, by my belt. That same evening I resigned. The next day I was a waiter at the Square Café, at Gisèle's mother's. Twelve cups broken. But dry feet.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai cousu ma première robe: At twelve, I sewed my first dress, for my mother, with the fabric scraps from her workshop: forty pieces in forty colours. She wore it to the palace ball. The old Archduchess asked her the name of her dressmaker. My mother answered: “She's twelve.” The next day, I had three orders.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai fait ma première babou: At twelve, I made my first babouches, a yellow pair, for my father. One size too small. He put them on without a word and wore them for a whole year. He limped a little, he smiled a lot. When people asked him why, he said: “My son made them.” I knew why he was limping.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai fait ma première bière: At twelve, I made my first beer all by myself: half-baked barley loaves crumbled into water, dates for sweetness, and patience. I forgot the patience. My beer was so sour that even the flies wouldn't touch it. My father took a sip, smiled and said: “Tomorrow, you start again.” I've been starting again for thirty years.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai fait ma première tarte: At twelve, I made my first pumpkin pie all by myself. Burnt underneath, raw on top. Grandma ate two slices without a word, then she showed me: the pastry, the oven, the nutmeg. Just a pinch. Even today, when I make it, I count under my breath like she did. One pinch. Not two. Pyra, don't start.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai joué au concert de l'A: At twelve, I played at the Academy concert. Well, I should have. In front of the packed hall, my fingers froze. Not one note, {surnom}. Not a single one. It has never left me. I still play every evening, at home, windows shut. And at the Fair, my piano plays in my place, pin by pin, exactly like me. It's my brass courage.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai percé un coquillage av: At twelve, I pierced a shell with a sea-urchin spine and threaded it onto fishing line. I gave it to my mum. She wore it to the market, a lady from Port-Azur wanted it, she paid two coins. Two coins! The next day, I had a stall. A plank on two rocks, but a stall.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai ramassé un caillou au: At twelve, I picked up a pebble by the pond. I swapped it for a feather, the feather for a piece of string, the string for… eight swaps later, I had a fishing rod! I traded it to young Moustache, who still fishes with it, forty years on. That day, I understood: a chain always ends well. Sometimes with whiskers.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai trouvé au grenier l'ap: At twelve, I found my grandfather's camera in the attic — an old one, with leather bellows. It didn't work any more. It took me two years to fix it, with parts bought in Port-Azur and lots of patience. My first photo was the Azur lighthouse, at night, seen from the beach. A little blurry smudge. I've still got it.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai vendu mon premier arti: At twelve, I sold my first item: a crab. It didn't want to be sold, it pinched the customer, and the customer paid for it anyway, on principle. That day I understood that you don't sell an object, you sell a story. The crab was a “guard crab”. The customer was delighted.
textes.À douze ans, j'ai vendu mon premier tapi: At twelve, I sold my first carpet. A little blue one, with a flaw in the corner. The customer offered a price: no. A second: no. At the third, I said: “For you, brother's price.” He went off delighted, and so did I. Since then, never the first price. The first price is for people in a hurry. The third is for friends.
textes.À douze ans, je me suis cachée dans la c: At twelve, I hid in the hold of a coaster carrying onions. When they found me, we were too far out to take me back. The captain put a bucket in my hands. Three years scrubbing the deck, and I knew everything: the winds, the knots, and that a captain who shouts isn't a captain who commands.
textes.À douze ans, je remontais ma première pe: At twelve, I brought up my first pearl. At fifteen, my first piece of the Léviathan: a bronze pulley, all green, with a letter engraved on it, a K. For Kerhervé, maybe. The coral and pearls, I sell to Salomé. The pieces of the ship, I keep. They belong to Carène, not to me.
textes.À douze ans, mon père m'a donné son mart: At twelve, my father gave me his hammer. He said: “Iron doesn't lie. If you cheat with it, it breaks.” I forged horseshoes for ten years. Then I went to sea, to see. On Balafre, there are no horses. So I make hooks, sabres, anchors. And nails. Lots of nails.
textes.À douze ans, une lettre est arrivée au m: When I was twelve, a letter arrived at the mill. Not by boat: by the wind, all by itself, stuck against the window. It just said: “Arcanelle. Come.” No signature! I left the next day with my umbrella and a loaf of bread. The umbrella is still in my room. The loaf, I ate on the way, with the seagulls.
textes.À genoux ! … Bon, pas la peine, le sol e: Kneel! … Well, no need, the floor is cold. By the power vested in me by… myself, I name you Honorary Squire of Montjoie! Here is your pay.
textes.À huit ans, Pomme-de-Pin a confié une le: When she was eight, Pomme-de-Pin handed a letter to the Post Office. Address: “The Moon”. She was asking if the moon wanted a bridge. I was already helping my father at the counter. I couldn't leave a letter unanswered. I wrote: “Yes, thank you, no rush.” Signed: the Moon. She pretends she didn't recognise my handwriting. A postmistress says nothing.
textes.À huit ans, j'ai couru avec ma première: At eight, I ran with my first flame and it went out. I came back in tears. Brother Cendrin knelt down, relit my wick and told me flames are carried like secrets: gently, and without running. He walked me back to the door, at my pace. He walks very slowly. It was perfect.
textes.À huit ans, j'ai écrit une lettre à la l: When I was eight, I wrote a letter to the moon, to ask if it wanted a bridge. I handed it in at the Post Office. Three days later, the reply arrived! The moon said: “Yes, thank you, no rush.” In very slanted handwriting, like an owl's. I have absolutely no idea who could have written it. Absolutely none.
textes.À huit ans, je suis allée chercher ma pr: At eight, I went to fetch my first flame from the Heart-Brazier, for a lantern I'd made myself. I ran. The flame went out on the way. I came back in tears. Brother Cendrin told me: “A flame is carried like a secret: gently, and without running.” I've never run with a flame since.
textes.À huit ans, à la Fête du Cristal, j'ai é: When I was eight, at the Crystal Festival, I sneezed. Every candle in the courtyard lit up, plus two hats and a bit of old Gaudence's beard. Séraphine took me by the ear, gently but firmly, and said: “You, you're coming to the Academy tomorrow.” I came. I never sneezed like that again. Well, hardly ever.
textes.À l'Académie, Malachar a voulu prouver q: At the Academy, Malachar wanted to prove that a flame could climb a staircase all by itself. I held the candle. The flame climbed the stairs, then the curtains, then the roof beams. The tower burned right up to the roof. We were both punished. Three centuries later, he still says I held the candle too close.
At the Academy, I was Héloïse's pupil. She gave me the problems nobody could solve, just to see. At twenty, I trapped a bolt of lightning in a bottle. A real one, crackling against the glass. I showed it to Héloïse at midnight; she came to the door in her dressing gown, monocle and all. Doctor the following year. And Héloïse got me the Volta laboratory.
textes.À l'Académie, j'étais le premier en tout: At the Academy, I was top in everything. One evening, I wanted to prove to my classmate Cendrin that a flame can climb a staircase by itself. It climbed it, then the curtains, then the rafters. The tower burned down. We were both punished. It was his candlestick. It was my idea. We each stick to our own version.
textes.À l'Académie, je suis assis à côté d'Ort: At the Academy, I sit next to Ortie. She knows everything, she lights candles from ten paces away, and she corrects me when I get it wrong. I teach her the names of mushrooms. Headmaster Malachar has wings and sees everything from up high. Miss Sulfura is nice, even when my fireflies fly off.
textes.À l'Académie, je suis la meilleure en fl: At the Academy, I'm the best at flames. Miss Sulfura gives me extra lessons, in the evening, in secret. Pépin sits next to me: he never knows his lesson, but he knows the names of forty mushrooms. I help him with his homework. He helps me with… um… he's very nice.
textes.À l'enterrement d'Honoré, Ambroise et mo: At Honoré's funeral, Ambroise and I stood on either side of the coffin. Two hours in the rain. Not a word. At the end, he raised his hat, I raised mine, and we each went our own way. Twenty-two years later, we're still at the hat stage. There's been no progress.
textes.À l'est, la forêt des brumes : mousse, m: To the east, the misty forest: moss, pools and fog. Plants I don't know. To the south, the desert: there's a cactus there whose sap makes you sleep. To the north, heather and thyme. The island is a pharmacy, you just have to know how to read it.
textes.À l'exercice des bougies, je devais en a: In the candle exercise, I was supposed to light just one. I snapped my fingers once, and all thirty candles in the courtyard lit up! Well, then I also set fire to Miss Sulfura's shoes. She gave me twenty out of twenty for precision and zero for discretion. That's an average of ten. It's scientific.
textes.À l'heure ! Ça devient rare. Les gens d': On time! That's getting rare. People here live “more or less”. You, you've got a pendulum. I'm keeping an eye on you, in the good way.
textes.À l'heure dorée, il s'assoit à côté de m: At the golden hour, he sits beside my easel and tells me about islands he's never seen: the golden trees of the elves, the dwarves' smoking mountain, the city under its bubble. He describes them so well that I paint them without seeing them. We travel together without leaving the bench.
textes.À l'heure dorée, je lui décris les îles: At the golden hour, I describe to her the islands I've never seen: the elves' platforms in the Mother Tree, the smoking Fire Mountain, the city under its bubble. She paints as she listens. Her islands look like nothing real. They look exactly like my maps.
textes.À l'heure où il raconte, je perce. J'ent: When he tells his tales, I'm piercing. I hear the beginning from the workshop, then a tricky hole takes hold of me, and the ending slips away. Even the tale he made about me, the night I relit the square. The children told me the ending: apparently I fly from lantern to lantern with a taper between my teeth. I don't fly. I haven't denied it.
textes.À l'heure pile, encore. Mon horloge et v: On time to the second, again. My clock and you would have made quite a pair.
textes.À l'inauguration du centième balayeur, t: At the unveiling of the hundredth sweeper, the whole city was on the Grand Square. The sweeper started singing, out of tune, the song Rivet hums while welding. There was a silence. Then a laugh, just one, then the whole square. I looked around for Rivet. He already had his back turned, and he was walking away.
textes.À l'inauguration du nouveau quai, j'ai v: At the opening of the new quay, I decided to sing my speech. A modern idea! By the second verse, Django had pulled out a tambourine and started banging. Loudly. Louder and louder. He calls that “accompanying”. Nobody heard a word. I was congratulated on my brevity.
textes.À l'odeur ? Bon, c'est pas faux. Un pois: By the smell? Well, that's not wrong. A fresh fish smells of the sea, not of fish. But if you sniff my sea bream in front of the customers, I'll chase you off with a broom, eh!
textes.À l'ouest, c'est la Grotte des Champigno: To the west is the Bouncing Mushroom Cave. The big pink mushrooms make you bounce. Wheee!
textes.À l'œil ! Bravo ! Un œil bombé, brillant: By the eye! Bravo! A bulging, shiny eye that looks at you as if it's about to talk. If the eye is sunken, the fish is old. You've got the makings of a fishmonger, you have.
By the eye, it must shine.
textes.À la Foire, Margot est venue au stand, e: At the Fair, Margot came to the stand, looked at the engine for a long time, and asked me: “How many turns a day?” I said: “Eighty-six thousand four hundred.” She nodded, wrote something down, and left without a word. With a sad face. Why a sad face? It's a very good number.
textes.À la Foire, j'ai demandé à monsieur Cogn: At the Fair, I asked Mr Cogne how many turns a day his engine made. He said: “Eighty-six thousand four hundred, roughly!” I worked out the friction in my head. Afterwards I didn't say anything. I left. He thought I was bored. I wasn't bored. I was sad for him.
textes.À la dernière Foire, Margot s'est assise: At the last Fair, Margot sat down in front of the automaton, with a cushion under her to reach the board. Forty-one moves, the longest game in its history. On the thirty-fourth, it thought for eleven minutes; you could hear the cards clicking all over the stand. She lost. She said “logical” and shook the automaton's hand. I gave her an ivory pawn.
textes.À la dernière Foire, j'ai joué contre l': At the last Fair, I played against Mr Checkmate's automaton. I lasted forty-one moves. It's the longest game in its whole history. At one point it thought for eleven minutes. After that, I lost. I said: “Logical.” Mr Checkmate gave me an ivory pawn. I put it in Mum's marble box. It's the only one that doesn't roll.
textes.À la dernière Fête du Cristal, elle m'a: At the last Crystal Festival, she sat me next to Pyra, with a jug of water between us. The jug froze on my side. On hers, it boiled. Séraphine drank from the middle and said: “Lukewarm. Perfect.” She was making fun of us. I saw it. I said nothing. Neither did the lake.
textes.À la dernière Fête du Cristal, elle nous: At the last Crystal Festival, she sat us side by side, Borée and me, with a jug of water in between. I didn't do anything on purpose! The jug boiled on my side and froze on his. Séraphine drank from the middle, saying: “Lukewarm. Perfect.” She thinks we didn't notice she was making fun of us. We did.
textes.À la dernière Fête du Cristal, j'ai assi: At the last Crystal Festival, I sat Pyra and Borée side by side, at Berthe's, with a jug of water between them. By dessert, the jug had frozen on Borée's side and was boiling on Pyra's. I drank from the middle and said: “Lukewarm. Perfect.” They didn't laugh. Berthe keeps the cracked jug on her shelf.
textes.À la dernière fête de l'Aube, Caelan a q: At the last Dawn festival, Caelan left the stage in the middle of the ballad. Celebrë was left alone, her hands shaking. So I danced in front of her, for an hour, so that everyone would look at me and not at her hands. It's the most beautiful dance of my life. I've never danced it again.
textes.À la dernière fête de l'Aube, il y a cen: At the last Dawn festival, a hundred years ago, Caelan cut his finger on a broken string. He was bleeding, he was smiling, and he wouldn't let me remove the golden thread that had just been tied to his harp. I put the bandage on over it. Since then, I know who gave him that thread.
textes.À la dernière fête de l'Aube, mon ruban: At the last Dawn festival, my ribbon got wound around Haldir. He stood still a whole morning while they untangled him, without a word of complaint. The fastest messenger in the village, not moving a step. I think it's the nicest compliment anyone's ever paid me.
textes.À la dernière fête des Cousines, il y a: At the last Cousins' Festival, a hundred years ago, the sky fairies came down to visit us. I lit every lantern in the garden with a snap of my fingers, all at once! Queen Oriane leaned down and held out a twig of Yggdrasil to me. She said: “A branch chooses its fairy.” The branch leapt into my hand. My wand!
textes.À la dernière fête des Cousines, une pet: At the last Cousins' Festival, a little all-pink fairy lit every lantern in the garden with a snap of her fingers. She was still trembling. I held out a twig of Yggdrasil to her; the twig leapt into her hand. Pimprenelle shrieked so loudly that the lanterns went out. I laughed like I hadn't laughed in ages.
textes.À la dernière fête du port, j'ai promis,: At the last harbour festival, I solemnly promised: “The clock will be repaired before the end of the year!” Applause. In the front row, Hortense took out a little black notebook and wrote something down. Afterwards she told me: “Fourteen.” I promise twice per festival, at the opening and the closing. I didn't know anyone was keeping score.
textes.À la dernière page, elle soupire. Toujou: At the last page, she sighs. Every time. A great big sigh that makes the newspaper tremble. Tourists turn round, worried. I tell them: “It's the herbal tea, it's strong.” At the end of the year, she leaves me a jar of honey on the counter. It's for my silence. I know it is. I keep quiet anyway… almost.
textes.À la fin de chaque danse de la baleine,: At the end of every whale dance, Jacquot cries. Every evening. Big tears, on his moustache. He says they're tears of joy. The first time, I thought he'd hurt himself. Now I hold the last note a bit longer, to give him time to wipe his eyes before the square applauds.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, Cuauhtli a: At the fair of the longest day, Cuauhtli burned copal to greet the suns. A mountain of copal, bought from the merchant Tochtli, so fragrant that I coughed through my whole hymn. Rê must have heard me through the smoke. Cuauhtli said it was a fine offering. I said it was a cloud.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, Cuauhtli e: At the fair of the longest day, Cuauhtli and I argued for a whole hour: Kukulkan or Quetzalcóatl? Who saw the Feathered Serpent first? Néferet was listening. At the end, she said: “Where I come from, the serpent is the enemy of the sun.” We both fell silent. That had never happened before.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, elle a goû: At the fair of the longest day, she tasted my cacao, pulled a face, and poured a spoonful of honey into it. Into MY cacao! In front of everyone! I shouted so loudly that the three priests turned round. Since then, I don't serve her any more. Ever. She watches me drink mine with a little smile. She knows nothing. Nothing at all.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, elle m'a a: At the fair of the longest day, she brought me a codex, folded like a screen. It took me an hour to understand the story. A very sad story. She waited politely, then she turned the codex over: I was reading it upside down. It was a celebration. She laughed without a sound, like a true schoolteacher. Me, very loudly, like an old scribe.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, elle m'a m: At the Longest Day Fair, she showed me her loom: a strap around the waist, the other end tied to a tree, and you lean back to stretch the threads. I tried, very seriously. The tree won. I landed on my bottom in the grass. She laughed so hard she lost her feathers. I laughed too. Inside, then out loud.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, j'ai brûlé: At the fair of the longest day, I burned copal to greet the three suns. A lot of copal. Néferet coughed through her whole hymn, without ever stopping singing. At the end, she said to me: “Your gods heard you. Mine too. And all the way to Yaxché.” Her eyes were red. I didn't dare tell her the price.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, j'ai goûté: At the fair of the longest day, I tasted her cacao. Bitter! I put a spoonful of honey in it, to fix it. Ix Chab cried sacrilege in front of the whole fair. Since then, she refuses to serve me any. I only drank it once. But I remember it. With honey, it was very good. Don't tell her.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, j'ai vu le: At the fair of the longest day, I saw the linen of Tiyi, the weaver from Per-Hâpy. White. Only white. She held it up to the sun, and the sun shone right through it, so softly. I cried, in front of everyone. Me, who swears only by colours! Since then, I hide a white thread in everything I weave. For Tiyi. And for my name.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, on a fait: At the fair of the longest day, we held a contest: who could build a jar the fastest. Him with his wheel, me with my coils. He finished well before me. Then we set the two jars side by side. He looked at mine. For a long time. He said “Hm”. Then we drank together without talking. I think I won something. I don't know what.

At the Longest Day Fair, we held a contest: who could build a jar the fastest. Me with my wheel, him with his coils of clay. I finished first, by a mile. Then we looked at the two jars. His was rounder. I said nothing. He said nothing. We had a drink together, without talking. It was very good.
textes.À la foire du plus long jour, sur les ha: At the fair of the longest day, in the highlands, we compare our suns. Mine crosses the Duat in his boat; hers goes down to Xibalba, where the Twins played ball against the Lords. She asked me: “And your Rê, does he play ball?” I said no. She looked genuinely sorry for him.
textes.À la foire, Kinich a voulu prêter des po: At the fair, Kinich wanted to lend Tlaco some of Peek's hair, for the winter. I told him to touch Tlaco. He touched him: all warm! His eyes went wide. He said: “He's got a fire inside!” Peek' sulked all day. He thought we liked Tlaco better. We did like Tlaco better.
textes.À la foire, Pilli m'a présenté Tlaco, so: At the fair, Pilli introduced me to Tlaco, his hairless dog. Peek' sniffed him all over, very surprised. So was I. I offered to lend Pilli some of Peek's hair, for the winter. Pilli told me to touch Tlaco. I touched him: all warm! Like a stone in the sun! Peek' sulked all day.
textes.À la foire, j'ai voulu lui montrer mon m: At the fair, I wanted to show her my loom. I tied the strap around her waist and the other end to a tree. She leaned back, very hard, very serious. The tree held. Tiyi didn't. She landed sitting in the grass, with all her dignity. I laughed so hard my feathers fell off. She laughed too. On the inside, then on the outside.
textes.À la foire, je lui ai montré un codex. I: At the fair, I showed him a codex. He looked at it for a whole hour, nodding, very learned. Then he said: “What a sad story.” It was the story of a celebration. He was reading it upside down. I turned it over. He read it again, and laughed so loudly that the priests turned round. He said: “Where I come from, we read both ways.”
At the fair, we compare our suns. Hers sails all night through the world below, against a serpent. Ours goes down to Xibalba. I asked her if her sun played ball, like our Twins. She said no. I was sincerely sad for him. A night without a ball game is a long one.
textes.À la fête de l'Aube, Nessa dansait avec: At the Dawn festival, Nessa was dancing with one of Ilyria's ribbons. By early morning, the ribbon was wound around three trees, the fountain and me. It took a whole morning to untangle me. Nessa laughed. As for me, I didn't want them to untangle me too quickly.
textes.À la fête de l'Aube, quand ma corde a ca: At the Dawn festival, when my string snapped and Ilyria replaced it, I jumped off the stage to run after her. In the middle of the ballad. Celebrë had to sing alone for an hour, making up the words. They say it was her finest hour. She says it was her worst.
textes.À la fête de l'année, il lit l'hymne dev: At the New Year festival, he reads the hymn in front of the whole village. Last year, he skipped a line. I said it for him, very quietly, and everyone heard it. He raised a finger and declared: “I wanted to check that the priestess was following.” Then he reread the line. Louder than me.
textes.À la fête des Cousines, j'ai allumé tout: At the Cousins' Festival I lit all the lanterns at once, and I was trembling all over. The queen leaned down to me; she smelled of summer rain. She held out a twig of Yggdrasil, which leapt into my hand all by itself. I squealed so loudly the lanterns went out. All of them. She laughed.
textes.À la fête, il a voulu danser avec mon pl: At the festival, he decided to dance with my finest tray, to make people laugh. They laughed. The tray fell, and he danced on it. A dent as big as an egg. I spent three days straightening it. Hassan says the tray was prettier with the dent. Tac. Hassan says a lot of things.
textes.À la fête, maman danse. Elle tourne avec: At parties, mum dances. She spins with her apron, she claps her hands, she pulls faces, and everyone laughs. Even the caïd smiled, once, I saw him. Me, I pretend to be embarrassed. But really, I'd love to dance like her when I'm grown up. Except the faces.
textes.À la loyale ? Avec ma jambe de bois ? …: Fair and square? With my wooden leg? … You'll see how hard my wooden leg hits! If you win, the purse is yours. If I win, you buy a round. Come on!
textes.À la loyale ? Toi et moi, et personne ne: A fair fight? You and me, and nobody butts in? … Ha! Fine. Put your fists up!
textes.À la loyale ? Toi et moi, personne ne s': Fair and square? You and me, nobody butting in? … Ha! All right. Put 'em up!
textes.À la noce, il n'a pas dit un mot. Pas un: At the wedding, he didn't say a word. Not one, all day. I thought he was angry. In the evening, he'd gone, and on my chair was his indigo chèche, folded in four. Itto told me: “It means yes.” I wear it on launch days. The first time, my hands were blue for a month.
textes.À la plate-forme de Vénus, elle danse. M: At the Venus platform, she dances. Me, I can't. I move like when I hunt: slowly, back low, eyes ahead. She says I do the jaguar, and she laughs. The others laugh too. I keep going. She laughs again. That's why I keep going.
textes.À la première réunion du jury, j'ai fait: At the first jury meeting, I had “unbeatable” entered in the minutes, on the automaton's line. Three times, so nobody could miss it. Héloïse wrote all three. And under each one, in her small handwriting: “according to Mr Échec”. I asked for the note to be removed. She proposed a vote. I lost the vote. Four to one.
textes.À la première réunion du jury, j'ai prop: At the first jury meeting, I proposed three prizes instead of a single Cog of Honour. Ambroise stood up and dictated to the clerk: “The jury notes that the automaton is unbeatable.” Then he had it noted a second time. Then a third, “for the minutes”. The clerk asked whether he should underline it.
textes.À la prochaine fête, je tiens douze seco: Next festival, I'll hold out for twelve seconds.
Until the next tide! Or the one after. I'm in no hurry, I'm twenty-two years ahead.
textes.À la prochaine, {surnom}. Reviens avec d: See you next time, {surnom}. Come back with coins.
See you around. Or not. The sea will decide.
textes.À la réunion du jury, j'ai proposé d'ajo: At the jury meeting, I suggested adding a prize for smiles. Héloïse asked me, over her monocle, how I intended to measure it. I answered: “People smile thirty-four per cent more near my machine.” She wrote “to be studied”. After that, I voted for everyone. Myself included. She sighed for a very long time.
textes.À la sortie scolaire, j'étais censé phot: On the school trip, I was supposed to photograph the pupils in front of the museum. I photographed shoes. Blue ones, with little buttons. Twenty times. When the photos came back, the school asked where the children were. Sylvie looked at the photos, then at me: “Do you like my shoes?” We got married the following year.
textes.À la triche ?! (Il éclate de rire, et se: Cheating?! (He bursts out laughing, and his teeth gleam.) What a nasty thought! Who told you about me? Sylvain? Gontran? Jealousy and lies, my friend.
textes.À la veillée de Tazira, c'était un jeune: At the gathering in Tazira, he was a skinny young sailor who smelled of tar. He told stories better than he fished, he said: he hadn't caught a thing in three weeks. He told a thousand stories, me just one, twice. When I'd finished, he said: “Not bad, bear. But the second time was better.”
textes.À ma gauche, Karim et ses babouches. À m: On my left, Karim and his slippers. On my right, Samira, my fiancée: we're getting married in spring, if we can agree on the price. Mbarek brings me carpets from the oasis and ruins me by keeping quiet. Ba Sidi sends me curious folk who want to see the carpet of stars and buy nothing. And a pirate paid the first price. I don't want to talk about it.
textes.À ma première leçon de flammes, j'ai mis: At my very first flame lesson, I set Professor Malachar's beard on fire. He said: “Excellent! Now put it out.” It took me three minutes. He gave me the best mark in the class. For enthusiasm.
textes.À ma première leçon de flammes, à l'Acad: At my first flame lesson at the Academy, I snapped my fingers too hard, and Professor Malachar's beard caught fire. He said: “Excellent! Now put it out.” It took me three minutes, crying and laughing. He gave me the best mark of the year. That day, I decided to become a teacher.
textes.À ma première leçon, j'ai mis le feu à s: At my first lesson, I set his beard on fire. The whole class held its breath. He looked at me, very calm, his beard blazing like a torch, and said: “Excellent! Now put it out.” It took me three minutes. He gave me the best mark of the year. He's worn his beard short ever since. As a precaution, he says.
textes.À mains nues ? Tu changeras d'avis devan: Bare hands? You'll change your mind when you see my sword. It's expensive, but it's convincing.
textes.À merveille ! Le chaudron chante, les na: Wonderfully! The cauldron is singing, the dwarves are eating, nobody's burnt themselves. Well, hardly anybody.
textes.À midi pile, quand la machine siffle, Ta: At noon sharp, when the machine whistles, Tacquet raises his cup, just once, without a word, as if toasting the hour. I give him his coffee free whenever it's dead on time. So, every day. He says I'll ruin myself. I say it's the price of punctuality.
textes.À midi pile. À l'endroit ou à l'envers,: At noon on the dot. Forwards or backwards, as you like.
textes.À midi, je donne un coup de main à sa ch: At noon, I lend a hand at her stove. She puts in cinnamon, I put in chilli. When her back is turned, I add more chilli. When my back is turned, she adds more cinnamon. Customers say the Crâne Fendu's stew changes flavour depending on the hour. That's us. It's war.
textes.À midi, je grille des sardines sur le qu: At noon I grill sardines on the quay. When the car goes up, I slip two through the window, wrapped in a page of the Gazette. Ernest gets them up top, piping hot. He sends the page back down in the next car, folded into a boat. Ten years of that. I've got a fleet.
textes.À moitié ! Ha ! Comme Sans-Dents. Mais t: Half! Ha! Like Sans-Dents. But which half do you choose? That's the secret. Keep the finest one.
textes.À moitié, Coyotl ! Tlaco a bu l'autre mo: Half, Coyotl! Tlaco drank the other half!
textes.À moitié. Il y a un plancher, un pilote,: Half. There's a floor, a pilot, windows and coffee. Achille has none of that. Not even a roof. Especially not a roof.
textes.À mon premier combat dans l'Arène, j'ava: At my first fight in the Arena, I was so scared that I closed my eyes. I walked straight ahead, slowly, and my opponent stepped out of the arena all by himself, backwards, so as not to get squashed. The crowd roared. I opened my eyes and said: “Sorry.” Since then, I always say sorry. It brings good luck.
textes.À mon âge, chaque matin est un cadeau. M: At my age, every morning is a gift. Even rainy mornings. Especially rainy mornings: nobody asks me to work.
At my age, every knot is a victory.
textes.À mon âge, je mange lentement. Ça me lai: At my age, I eat slowly. It gives me time to take a second plate.
textes.À neuf ans, je suis allé voir l'Amirale: When I was nine, I went to see the Admiral to become a cabin boy. She said: “Ring the bell on time for a month, without a mistake.” I got it wrong four times. She took me on anyway. She said the four times were to check whether Carène was listening. She's kind, the Admiral. But secretly.
textes.À neuf ans, on m'a envoyé à la Maison de: At nine, I was sent to the House of Life. The master made me copy out the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor: a sailor is stranded on an island, and a giant serpent, covered in gold, talks to him very kindly. Three hundred times I copied it. I dreamed of chatty serpents. Even today, I recite it with my eyes closed. It puts the pupils to sleep. That's useful.
textes.À onze ans, ma première Grande Course. J: At eleven, my first Great Race. I shoot off like an arrow… and at the root bend, just before the Lookout, I fall. Twisted ankle. Pépin, who'd fallen too, carried me on his back to the finish. We came last, together. Last! Me! Since then, I've never finished behind anyone again. Hop.
textes.À personne ? Oh, mais il faut ! Ce n'est: To nobody? Oh, but you must! It's not forbidden to give some to yourself, you know. Here, next time, I'll give you one. You'll be your own first customer.
textes.À personne, et c'est bien ça le souci !: To no one, and that's the problem! It's Brioche. Ginger and white, like a golden brioche, see? Every morning at six, she comes down from the roof, takes ONE sardine from me, just one, very politely, and goes back up to eat it while watching me. She doesn't steal, she helps herself. She's dignified, that cat. More dignified than the mayor. But there it is: she has nobody. In winter, she sleeps against the harbour master's chimney, and Odette pretends not to see her. I can't take her, I have three floors and an allergic husband. You travel… A cat that travels, I think she'd like that. But she won't let anyone near her. Except… Pauline, the Grand Hotel's chambermaid, knits on the terrace: one day, Brioche came to play with her ball of yarn. She even purred. Go see Pauline!
textes.À quarante ans, Gunnar m'a parié une cho: When I was forty, Gunnar bet me a mug that I wouldn't go all the way to the edge of the crater. I went. Alone. I came back with a shard of obsidian and singed eyebrows. My uncle shouted for an hour, then he named me scout of the slopes. Gunnar still owes me that mug.
textes.À quarante ans, Lyra a voulu regarder pa: At forty, Lyra wanted to look over the mist, and she fell off the highest walkway. Ankle on backwards. I bandaged it with sage leaves and made her drink my potion. She pulled such a face that in the Bois-Doré they still say “to pull a Lyra face”. I take it as a compliment.
textes.À quarante ans, elle est montée au bord: At forty, she climbed to the rim of the crater on a dare. Alone. She came back down with a shard of obsidian and singed eyebrows. I shouted for an hour. Then I made her a scout. Now she shouts less than me. She learnt.
textes.À quarante ans, j'ai trouvé un petit cor: At forty, I found a little crow that had fallen in the ash, all lopsided, squawking louder than himself. I fed him cheese. He never left. He's the one who taught me to talk to crows. Well, to listen to them. That's Croâ. He says he's an eagle. He isn't.
textes.À quatorze ans, j'ai construit ma premiè: At fourteen, I built my first boat, all by myself, out of papyrus. I called her The Dragonfly. She floated to the middle of the river, very proud, then came apart like a badly plaited braid. I swam home pushing my basket of fish in front of me. My father said: “You swim well. Like your great-grandfather.”
textes.À quatorze ans, je suis allée frapper ch: At fourteen, I went and knocked on Professor Boum's door. He said: “Stand there. No, there. Further back.” I stayed six years. Four roofs. I swept up soot and dreamed of colours. He taught me to listen to a boiler: when it sings, all's well; when it goes quiet, you run. It's the best lesson of my life.
textes.À quatorze ans, je suis montée à l'Acadé: At fourteen, I went up to the Academy. The healing mistress was old Bourrache, who smelled of camphor and scolded plants that grew crooked. She taught me that you don't heal with your hands, but with your ears: you must listen before you touch. It took me ten years to understand. I'm not sure I've finished.
textes.À quatorze ans, un cirque est passé en v: At fourteen, a circus came to town: the Two Moons Circus. I saw a clown fall twelve times in a row, and everyone laughed, even my father, for one second. That very night I packed my bag. I carried buckets, fed the goats, and learned to juggle with potatoes. The goats ate the balls.
textes.À quinfe ans, f'ai embarqué fur un brick: At fifteen, I thigned on to a brig called the Theagull. I thcrubbed the deck, mended the netth, learned the knotth. Much later, Gontran bought her and renamed her the Thcarlet Widow. Me, I changed captainth, not thipth. Back then, nobody called me Thans-Dents. They called me Thébathtien. Ah, it wath a fine name, Thébathtien.
textes.À quinze ans, Tréphine m'a donné son car: At fifteen, Tréphine gave me her green journal, all warped with seawater. Three hundred recipes, half of them crossed out. “The crossings-out are what I learned,” she used to say. I set up the infirmary on the lower deck, between the hammocks: the patients are already lying down, it saves time.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai cousu un soufflet pou: At fifteen, I sewed a bellows for Jos's forge, my first job all on my own. The stitches were crooked. I've offered a hundred times to redo it. He always refuses: he says it blows better crooked. I mostly think he doesn't want to hurt my feelings. With Jos, you never know.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai embarqué avec Corenti: At fifteen, I went out with Corentin, who was a fisherman before he was a talker. He taught me to gut a mackerel in three moves, and then to say it weighed three pounds. The three moves, I forgot. The three pounds, never. That's how you become a real Carène fisherman.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai frappé à la cabane de: At fifteen, I knocked on Barnabé's hut. I wanted to know how he'd built it all by himself, after his shipwreck. He taught me sailors' knots, how to read the wind before putting up a roof, and that planks have a grain, like maps have a direction. He talked to Gaston the whole lesson. Gaston already knew everything.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai posé mon chapeau sur: At fifteen, I put my hat down on the Great Square and played. A single coin fell in. It was Grandpa Ébène's. He said: “Come and play behind my stories.” Since then, I play for him: low notes for the dragons, soft ones for the princesses, and a very long one when he forgets what comes next.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai pris la corde. Père a: At fifteen, I took the rope. Father said: “Are you sure?” I said: “Hrmm.” With me, it goes up in silence. The passengers came back. I know the story of every wicker changed. And every rope. Four wickers. Six ropes. One basket. Grandpa's.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai voulu inventer un car: At fifteen, I wanted to invent a fizzing caramel. It fizzed. Then it whistled. Then it took out the kitchen window and a good part of the ceiling. My mother, covered in sugar, looked at me for a long time, and advised me to charge for my explosions in future. Ten years later, I opened L'Alambic in her sweet shop. The shelves still smell of caramel.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais apprenti chez le v: At fifteen, I was apprenticed to the old polisher of the Upper Town. My first real client was Asmodin, the palace butler. He watched me work for an hour, without a word. Then he looked at himself in the mirror and said: “Acceptable.” I wept with joy. He still comes, every Monday. He still says “acceptable”.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais mousse. On est arr: At fifteen I was a cabin girl. We arrived here, Sel disguised as a salt merchant. The harbour women sold us sacks of sand. Sand! And a girl of twenty, Fatima, saw me skinny as a herring and gave me a bowl of harira. That night, I was the one carrying the lantern when Sel hid his chest in the caves. Where? Ha! Drink up.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais pêcheur, et longte: At fifteen, I was a fisherman, and for a long time I kept my boat alongside Driss's. At thirty-five, my father died, and the port gave me his staff. The first morning, I set the price of sardines. The whole port shouted: too high, too low, too early. I held firm. The next day, they shouted less. That's what being amin is: you listen to the shouting, then you decide.
textes.À quinze ans, je comptais les pièces plu: At fifteen, I counted coins faster than the eye could see them. A captain accused me of cheating in front of the whole room. My father put a coin on the table, hid it under three cups, and said: “Find it.” The captain lost ten times in a row. He left grumbling that I had silver fingers. The name stuck. The captain didn't.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis descendu au port a: At fifteen, I went down to the port with a bundle and a hammer. I learned iron from a blacksmith, wood from a carpenter, and money on my own. I'm the one who laid the keel of the Stubborn Seagull. Three years in the shipyard. On the day she sailed, the shipowner told me: “You built her, you fix her.” I came aboard. I shouldn't have.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis entré dans la mari: At fifteen, I joined the king's navy, lookout on the Faithful, a brand-new galleon. I had a copper spyglass and a uniform that was too big. For two years, I saw whales, islands, storms, and once a sea serpent. Nobody believed me. Nor did the serpent, I think: it left straight away.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis entrée à la Fabriq: At fifteen I joined the Works, apprenticed to Master Rivet. He didn't talk, he showed. And while welding he hummed an old shepherds' song, always out of tune, always the same one. It was with him that I made the Zéphyr: me the plans and the gas, him the giant sewing machine for the envelope. We were a very good machine, the two of us.
textes.À quinze ans, ma mère m'a laissé son tou: At fifteen, my mother left me her wheel. My first bowls all leaned the same way, as if they were listening to something. Then one day, they stood up straight. My first big tagine dish, I made it for my aunt Zineb, at the Fondouk. It's still there. She shows it to every caravan driver, and adds that I'm ready to marry. Thanks, khalti.
textes.À quinze ans, ma première traversée. Tro: At fifteen, my first crossing. Three days of sand, all the way to Tazira. On the last morning we crossed the last dune, and there was the sea. All blue, to the end of the world. The others talked, laughed, ran to the water. I sat down. I said nothing for an hour. My father said: “Good. He understood.”
textes.À quinze ans, mon oncle Pech, le vieil a: At fifteen, my uncle Pech, the old astronomer, took me into the observatory. He taught me Venus: she rises in the morning, disappears, rises in the evening, disappears, and comes back every five hundred and eighty-four days. I copied his tables into a folded bark book. It's there, in my niche. It smells of smoke, rain and old age. So do I.
textes.À quinze ans, on m'a confié le huehuetl: At fifteen, I was given the huehuetl in the square: a hollow trunk as tall as me, with a skin stretched over it. The first evening, I played so long I couldn't feel my hands. The dancers stayed until dawn. The next day, my hands were blue. Like the hips of the ball players of Yaxché.
textes.À réparer ? Bien. Le monde a besoin de g: Mend them? Good. The world needs people like you. And glue. If one day you have a cracked pot, bring it along: I'll show you how to stitch clay back together.
textes.À sa première leçon, la petite Sulfura a: In her first lesson, little Sulfura set my beard alight with a snap of her fingers. The whole class froze. I said: “Excellent! Now, put it out.” It took her three minutes, crying and laughing at the same time. I gave her the best mark of the year. As for my beard, it never grew back as long.
textes.À sa première nuit, elle avait seize ans: On her first night she was sixteen, with trembling knees. Just as she was lifting the moon out of the pond, she stumbled, and the whole Circle held its breath. I whispered to her from my moss: “You don't lift it, little one. You rock it.” She rocked. Since then, she's the one.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai fabriqué ma première p: At sixteen, I made my first sap potion, with herbs from my mother's garden. I tasted it myself, on principle. My eyes turned green. They stayed that way, and they glow a little in the dark. It's very handy for reading labels at night. I've never regretted it.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai fait mon propre ras-el: At sixteen, I made my own ras el hanout. Thirty-two spices, weighed to the grain. And a thirty-third ingredient that nobody knows. My mother smelled it, smiled, and said nothing. The caravan men bought three sacks and took it all the way to Carène. My blend saw Carène before I did. It travels better than me: it doesn't complain.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai lu une annonce de Lumi: At sixteen, I read an advert from Lumina: “Seeking someone who isn't afraid of the night.” I went to see her. I only said three words: “I like night.” She gave me a pole and the list of street lamps. Since then, I've lit up the city every evening. I've given every lamp a name. Gustave flickers when he's happy.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai poussé la porte du Pai: At sixteen, I pushed open the door of the Pain Doré to buy a baguette. I made a big gesture while talking and knocked over a whole basket of croissants. Margaux looked at me and said: “You've got energy, you. Can you knead?” The next day, at four in the morning, there I was, in an apron.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai pris la pierre de ma g: At sixteen, I took my grandmother's stone and went down alone. I brought back pearly shells, sea urchins, once an old silver spoon. Now I dive for Momo's necklaces, for curious folk, for me. Underwater, there's no time. That's why I lose track of it up here too.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai quitté la confiserie a: At sixteen, I left the sweet shop with a box of humbugs and three bone dice. On the harbour, some sailors were playing on a barrel. I sat down. By morning, I had their coins, their caps and a place on their boat. Since then, I've never had a real job. Dice, my friend, are better than a job: they're a conversation with luck.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai suivi une caravane jus: At sixteen, I followed a caravan all the way to the oasis, my sardine tin on my back. There, an old musician listened to me and laughed. Then he made me a real guembri: a wooden neck, a stretched camel skin, three strings. He told me: “Inside, you must put the desert night.” It took me two years to understand.
textes.À seize ans, j'avais mon numéro : la Rou: At sixteen, I had my own act: the Redhead and Her Blades. Marcel, my partner, stood on a big spinning wheel, and I planted the knives all around him, a finger's width away. One evening, in front of three hundred people, with the wheel spinning, he asked me for a raise. I raised a knife, thought about it, and put it down. I changed careers that very night.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré en apprentiss: At sixteen, I was apprenticed to Honoré Cogne, the greatest automaton maker in Cliquetis. Thirty years in the workshop. As my old master used to say: “A gear never lies. It's the clockmaker who lies.” He started the chess-playing automaton, then he died, twenty-two years ago, without finishing it. The workshop and the automaton were left to me. The golden gear, to his grandson.

At sixteen, I was apprenticed to an old clockmaker on the Grand Square. Forty-two years later, I still have fine oil under my fingernails. For thirty years, I've kept and wound the great clock of the Academy, every morning at seven. I sleep with three alarm clocks. They ring at the same second. If one of them lags, I don't sleep for a week.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré à l'école de: At sixteen, I joined the Guard school. I was the tallest, the most serious, and the clumsiest with a sword. My instructor said I fought like a drawbridge: slowly, but nobody gets past. I took it as a compliment. I still take it that way.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré à la Fabrique: At sixteen, I joined the Works as Master Rivet's apprentice. Sweepers, carriers, arms, wheels. Master Rivet doesn't say much. He shows you. He puts a part in front of you, says “Hm”, and you understand. Or you start again. I started again a lot. In the end, I understood.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entrée chez la viei: At sixteen, I went to work for old Madame Carillon, who made music boxes on Springs Street. She taught me cylinders and pins: one pin, one note; one crooked pin, a wrong note forever. When she passed away, she left me her tools, with a little note: “Plant straight.”
textes.À seize ans, les genoux de maman n'ont p: At sixteen, Mum's knees gave out. I danced alone for the first time. Oh… I was so scared. When it came to lifting the moon out of the pond, I stumbled. Mother Moon whispered to me: “You don't lift it, you rock it.” Since then, I'm the dancer. Mum lives in peace with the does of the deep forest. I visit her every season.
textes.À seize ans, ma mère m'a offert un métie: At sixteen, my mother gave me a loom, an old one that creaked like an inn door. I spent a whole winter at it. Silk, cotton, northern wool, and the desert dyes. The first cloth, I laid against my mother's cheek. She closed her eyes and said: “Soft as a cloud.” I've said it to all my customers ever since. It's hers.
textes.À seize ans, un caboteur s'est arrêté su: At sixteen, a coaster stopped at our island for fresh water. Its helmsman had a fever, and nobody knew how to steer. I raised my hand: I'd learned on my father's boat. I brought the coaster to the next port without a scratch. The skipper kept me on. The crew called me Winkle. I protested. It lasted six years.
textes.À seize ans, une vieille tatoueuse est p: At sixteen, an old tattooist came by the shipyard. She had anchors on her arms, fish on her hands and a little dragon behind her ear. I followed her for three years, from port to port, preparing her inks. She used to say: “Skin isn't canvas. It breathes, it moves, it remembers.” When she left for good, she left me her needles.
textes.À sept ans, j'ai inventé la cuillère. J': At seven, I invented the spoon. I'd drawn it all: a handle, a little hollow at the end… My grandmother handed me a spoon. Without a word. At nine, I invented the kite. At ten, the sock. I've always had my ideas… just after everyone else. My grandmother said I was one idea behind. Just one. That's not much, one idea.
textes.À sept ans, je suis entrée au temple. Am: At seven, I entered the temple. Amenemhat, who still had hair back then, taught me the signs. He had me copy out the morning hymn, again and again. One day, I drew a little sleeping cat in the margin, to rest. He said nothing. He kept the papyrus. He still shows it to visitors, thirty-eight years later.
textes.À sept ans, mon grand-père m'a emmenée d: When I was seven, my grandfather took me into the cave, under the great ridge. He showed me the round stone, carved all over. I took out my little screwdriver to take it apart. I couldn't. It's the only thing in the world I've never managed to take apart. It was warm, {surnom}. Like a hand. I still dream about it. The last time I went up, black brambles were blocking the cave.
textes.À six ans, j'ai fait mon premier grand c: At six, I made my first big hip shot. The ball flew over the wall and landed on the head of Ah Kin Pech, who was watching Venus. It bounced and landed back on mine! Two identical bumps. Everyone says he's the one who saw stars. I saw them too. But I don't admit it.
textes.À six heures ? C'était tout doux, à six: At six? It was ever so gentle, at six!
textes.À soixante ans, j'ai suivi une chèvre ég: At sixty, I followed a stray goat all the way to the fumaroles. In the hot ash, there were little red glimmers. I bit into one. I sneezed a flame, I cried, I laughed, and I knew I had my stew. The white ones, I tasted those too. A week of being a dragon. Never again.
